When Harm is gone, the tin cannot be found, but when Harm later pays the thatchers, he takes it out from under the reeds again. According to the narrator, this is the devil's work. When Harm died he did not have a cent, but during his life he had a great deal. He looks like a tramp, with filthy rags on his body. When work is being done on the narrator's little house, he asks how much he has to pay for it. As a joke the narrator names a high sum and Harm simply pulls a pile of paper money from his pocket. The narrator says they were afraid of Harm because he was the devil's child. He is cruel and nearly murdered his wife Jeltsje. Harm has a wisseldaalder (a coin that always returns). He pays with it, and a little later the recipient has lost all the money, because the coin always comes back to Harm along with the rest of the money. That is why he is so rich. Once someone received money from him. The man holds the money tightly in his fist, but when he reaches the Wilde Pad, the money is no longer there.
16099: Harm the Stutterer was the brother of a witch who had once been shot through the throat in the form of a three-coloured cat. The man who shot her still often tells the story.
16101: One night Harm the Stutterer was groaning and writhing outside in the field, crying in a horrible voice that he was being beaten to death. The narrator, passing by, told him there was no one there. A little later Harm was raving with pain again. It was the devil who had got hold of him.
16109: The narrator says that when they were children and got something from a witch, an apple or something else, their mother always made them throw it away, because such an apple turned into a toad.
16110: A man from the neighbourhood once came to tell the narrator's mother that his daughter was being treated badly by her husband. While talking he would not sit down. Later he explained why he kept standing. The house had been completely full of people from a funeral. A few weeks later a sister of the narrator died. The man had seen it all beforehand when he came to talk about his daughter.
16121: One evening the narrator saw lots of lights from her parental home. Her mother then said that a busy road might well come there. Two or three years later that road came.
16122: One evening the narrator's husband went to Drachtster Compagnie with three mates. On the Folgerster laan a very eerie black dog came along, with glowing eyes as big as tea saucers and a very long tail. It crept right past them. All four of them had seen it and their legs shook with fear. It was a plaagbeest (tormenting beast).
16126:
If magpies sit chattering in a tree by a house, someone will die.
If the dog howls eerily, someone will die.
If the cat washes itself, visitors are coming.
16131: Boardzer Bruining (son of Thomas Klare, see: Kollumerzwaag) lives at Houtigehage and was born with a caul. One night he had to go out; he was woken. When he came home he was as white as buttermilk. He had seen a funeral procession. There was a puddle on the road and the horse stepped around it. That same week a funeral procession came by and the horse walked around the water.
16143: Antsje Jongsma had a wisseldaalder (a coin that always returns).
16157: Johannes Meerstra from Veenwouderwal can do more than an ordinary person. They always call him Johannes kaas (Johannes cheese) or kaasloper (cheese seller). He can make women's skirts drop or make fire tongs dance. The narrator once simply sails with him from Veenwouden to the Wal, which no person can do. Johannes is a Freemason and has sold himself to the devil. He can make little soldiers come out of the hearth pit, and cats too.
16159: The narrator's father once told of a girl who was in service with a farmer. She got a sweetheart, and when she sat with her fiancé in the back of the house in the evening, something would suddenly leave her and she would turn deathly pale. After an hour, something that looked like a swarm of gnats came in through a drain hole. They went into her mouth. She was a nightmare and had been out to torment other people. When it happened for the third time, the fiancé told the farmer and she was dismissed.
16165: If magpies chatter, visitors are coming. If dogs howl eerily, a corpse is coming.
16264: A foal with a porridge pot around its neck runs along the Goddeloze Singel.
16268: If the wreath is burnt, the witch dies.
16488: Klaas Kunst can crawl through a beam. But someone in the audience notices that it is an illusion: he crawls past it.
16491:
In Bergumerheide a child of Sikke Maei was bewitched. Now and then a strange cat haunted the house. Then Maei threw a kettle of hot water at the cat. The next day Frearke Jel had her head in a cloth. Frearke Jel was a witch. She went from house to house selling laces, ribbon and thread.
When Frearke had bewitched children, they stood upright in the cradle and became as stiff as a board. Later they became as limp as a rag.
16492: The white gate by the Puntbos in Bergumerheide was haunted.
16493: A wizard fixed dogs to the spot. They could move on again when he touched the cart. He could also do ventriloquism.
16497: Near the old churchyard of Bergumerheide on the Earmhústerwei someone once hanged himself. Since then the place has not been right. There is a gate there that always opens by itself, and at night between twelve and one a flock of white chickens is seen.
16498: A few men were coming back from Leeuwarden one night. Alle Putter (=Jager) was with them too. Near Bergumerheide he said: "Men, step aside, or we'll stumble. There's a funeral procession coming." When the funeral procession had passed, they went back to walking in the middle of the road. He was the only one who had seen it. A week later there was a real funeral procession.
16499: In Zwagerbosch there lived a man who very often had to go out at night. Once he had to go out again. Fedde, the second husband of Thomas Klare, had died then. The man saw Fedde's funeral procession. Some people followed him. All the gates opened for him. So he had to see it.
16502:
There was a farmhand who had made a pact with the devil. He once bet the farmer that he could spread out molehills in three hours. He calmly lay down in the field to sleep, and within three hours everything was black. The devil had done it.
The same fellow was once near Dokkum with a few others. They cursed and raged. The next day they were on a heap of hay on the other side of the canal. One of them would sometimes whistle and then the devil came.
He could also make someone stand naked.
He could make his wife fly through the air. When he began reading in his book of magic, rooks flew out of the hearth pit. Once they found him dead in the hay bay with his head turned backwards. The book of magic he had burned completely, but a short time later it lay in a chest again.
16504: Bearn Smook from Feansterheide had fought with the devil. He lay beaten black and blue in a ditch. The devil was a small little man.
16505: In Folgeren there was a gate where at night a foal stood with a porridge pot around its neck.
16507: In Kollumerzwaag there lived a labourer who had to see everything. At night he would go out and run through the gates. They opened for him by themselves. In no time he was at the place where he had to be, as if he flew. Then he saw the funeral procession. He always knew who was going to die, but he never said.
16508: One night a man saw someone coming towards him on the Feansterheide. He said good evening but got no answer. Then he saw the funeral procession coming. The man had been its forerunner.
16509:
Next to the house in Zwaagwesteinde where the narrator lived in her youth lived a woman who had been born with a caul. Once she said that one of her boys would die. At night she had seen the coffin standing in the wrong corner of the room, because otherwise it could not be turned. Half a year later one of the neighbour's sons did indeed die. It went exactly as she had seen it.
Another time she had seen the narrator's parental home burning. Less than three months later it burned down. What that woman saw always came true.
16510: The narrator's father was once going back from Sânbulten to Zwaagwesteinde at one o'clock at night. In the Zwagerbosch he suddenly saw five women standing there wearing pointed caps and long white skirts. There was not a breath of wind, yet the plumes of the caps waved to and fro. He was frightened to death and went to old Bearn's farm. When they went to look together, the women were gone.
16511: In Zwaagwesteinde, close to Twijzelerheide, lived Anne and Hiltsje. Anne drank a lot and often came home blind drunk. He treated Hiltsje like a dog. When she died, he put an old barrel on the grave instead of a gravestone. But then Hiltsje came to haunt him every evening. In the end he no longer dared to be in his own house at night.
16512: Old Harm (the Stutterer) of the Wyldpad was a sorcerer. He had a wisseldaalder (a coin that always returns).
16515: A bargeman's hand walks in the dark along a path across the churchyard near Buitenpost. He is thrown to the ground three times in a row.
16516: In the west of Buitenpost, in the lanes on either side of the military police barracks, a foal with a porridge pot around its neck used to run.
16517: The narrator's uncle had heard the heavy vehicles beforehand that later came to drive on the Groningen highway. They were exactly the same sounds.
16519: The narrator's parents lived in Kollumerpomp. They often had labourers and fellows who told ghost stories. Once one of them told that the Godshuis stood on the Oosterboereweg near Kollum. It was a labourer's cottage. There stood a stallion's hoof and a goat's hoof. If you passed by at eleven o'clock at night, a voice was heard saying: stop, no further. That was the voice of the devil.
16520: A man is turned down by a girl. He is in a foul temper and curses and swears horribly. He is punished for it. On the way home a young fellow comes walking beside him. It is the devil. The man becomes so frightened that the sweat drips off him. The little fellow stays with him all the way home.
16521: Japik, the storyteller's husband, is coming back from Twijzel with some friends. They are boasting and cursing as they walk, until the devil comes walking beside them. He follows them to the door. They are scared to death, except Japik, because he has a clear conscience.
16522: On the Swâdde three dog's paws and a horse's hoof can always be seen. The horse's hoof belongs to the devil. The storyteller has often seen these prints.
16523: Harm, the Stammerer, has buried a pot of money in the ground. Sometimes his nephew Sjoerd has to help him get to it, because then the devil is with it. His nephew Jan lived with him. They slept in the same bed. One night there is tripe lying in Harm's place. Harm himself had gone out to practise witchcraft.
16525: At Karste Harmke's the chickens sometimes sit back to front. Their heads are turned around. The devil rules there.
16534: In Den Andel there is a haunted barn. A woman has been seen at the window with a face as white as chalk and her hair hanging limp around it.
16769: As a child, the narrator feels threatened at night by something that must have been a nightmare. After his father puts some substance in a piece of paper under his pillow, he is no longer troubled by it.
16776: The narrator meets a funeral procession around midnight.
16778: A group of boys is on its way home at night, noisy and cursing. At a gate one of the boys is suddenly seized and is later found charred on the road.
16779: A man who always goes home alone late at night boasts that he is not afraid. One evening a big man suddenly stands in front of him and does not answer his greeting. When he threatens to hit him, he himself is thrown to the ground so roughly that he has to crawl home.
16780: From a group of boys standing together, someone is suddenly snatched up without them seeing who did it. The boy was never seen again.
16782: A drunken braggart is thrown from one ditch into the other on his way home.
16783: Example of a woman with a plaagbeest (tormenting creature) in her body. Her suitor sees the plaagbeest disappear through the window, after which the woman can no longer speak. As soon as the plaagbeest is back in her body, she can speak again. Such a woman has been sold to the evil one.
16807: Walking home one evening, a father tells his son to walk behind him, so they will not step into the paw prints of the roaming black dog, a plaagbeest (tormenting beast).
16808: A woman selling bread was pushed to the side of the road, cart and all.
16809: A paraffin peddler is a wizard who drives his paraffin cart through the keyhole.
16810: When a cat is struck, a woman who can change into anything and get through anything is injured the next day.
16812: In revenge because a man lets his dog keep attacking a man, the latter fixes the man and the dog to the spot.
16813: Dancers are fixed to the spot by a farmhand and cannot move a foot.
16818: A shopkeeper from Hamsterheide can make little soldiers come out of the hearth pit. He tells the children who come into his shop that they may come and watch. One evening they come. He calls up the little soldiers and has them drill.
16819: One evening people see a farm in Drogeham on fire. They go there, and the further they get, the fiercer it burns. But when they reach the Ham, the fire is out. The farm is still standing. But it is sure to burn down one day.
16820: One evening the narrator sees the water mill at the Wide Petten on the Polderdyk ablaze. But the next morning it is still standing. The following year, however, the mill caught fire during a storm. The narrator had already seen it a year beforehand.
16824: A plaagbeest (tormenting beast) is a kind of foal with big eyes that haunts the place. A man who came across one near a farm never dared to pass there again.
16826: Suddenly a big, fat sheep stands by a house with its head against the roof. The neighbour woman sees this and goes to ask where it came from. But the son of the house denies that they have been given a fat sheep. The neighbour goes outside to look again and then the sheep is gone. When she comes back in, the boy's mother is suddenly home. She had been the sheep herself. Now the neighbour knows that she is a witch.
16827: If someone is ill and will soon die, the dogs howl.
16828: One evening a woman is suddenly knocked off the road. She had walked into a hearse and fallen.
16829: A woman often has to go out in the evening to see something. Once she sees a coffin standing in the middle of a narrow path. A cart could just get past. Later someone in the neighbourhood dies there. Another time she sees a wheelbarrow with a coffin in which no one was lying. The man for whom the coffin was meant died a few days later.
16834: A woman is catching moles on the land with the eerie tree of the Bomklooster. Suddenly, some distance from her, two witte juffers (white maidens) walk across the land. When she goes over to look, they have vanished like snow before the sun.
16836: One evening a woman is coming back from milking. Suddenly she is thrown into a ditch, milk and all. It had been a funeral procession that swept her off the road.
16837: An old woman is pushed off a path. She ends up in a ditch. It was caused by a funeral procession. Some time later a real funeral procession went along the same path to the churchyard.
16840: Uncle Piter was a knife grinder; he was murdered on the Wildpad on the Twizelerheide. Our dad saw that murder happen at night while he lay in bed. He thought: I know that person, but he could not see his face. There was a thunderstorm. He got out of bed and was completely beside himself. However hard he tried to see who was being murdered, he could not. From the bearing and build he clearly saw that he knew the person. That same day he received the news: it was his brother.
16841: Father and mother were sailing. They moored at the Rolbrug on the Tynje side. They go to sleep. By the rudder of the ship something starts to move and comes up out of the water. And it keeps going up and down. That same night they sailed away. Later mother asked what it had been. A postman had drowned at that spot.
16842: Father is a merchant. People call him Tseard Kuorke. He often travels with Uncle Piter. They are young fellows. They travel from one lodging house to another. They stay at Terwindsel's lodging house. Jan Kluwer is staying there too, a big, strange-looking fellow. He is a knife grinder and has a magic coin. Father and Uncle tease him. He gets angry and says they won't sleep a wink that night; he will make the horses dance. They have barely gone to bed when the noise starts. They cannot get to sleep. Uncle Piter is not afraid. He jumps out of bed and goes to Jan Kluwer, who looks up startled. Jan Kluwer is bathed in sweat. "If you don't stop soon," says Piter, "you'll die here under my hands." Suddenly the horses are quiet.
16843: Janne is the name of the landlady of the boarding house. All vagrants find shelter there. They have to pay in advance. Janne has an old man as a boarder. He cannot eat quickly. Janne does not wait for him. She ladles the porridge onto the plate while the potatoes are still on it. One day Jan Kluwer comes to Janne's boarding house. He cannot pay her. He gets no lodging. Jan Kluwer leaves. Uncle Piter follows him. Jan Kluwer walks around a tree three times. He mutters something. He digs with his hands in the earth under the tree. Uncle Piter cannot see what he takes from the ground. Jan Kluwer is sweating heavily. He goes back to the boarding house and throws a purse of money on the table. Jan Kluwer pretends to be poor, but he always has money. He is a Freemason and has a magic coin.
16844: A man is at a neighbourhood meeting in Skieding. Someone there said: "I come through Mearumer Leech and three lanterns are burning there." A year later three stops for the tramline are built there.
16846: During the mobilisation of 1918, when the Spanish flu is raging, a man and a child set out early in the morning. One day they come to the churchyard of Beets. Magpies are flying everywhere there. They cannot be driven away. The man senses that something is happening and wants to go home. On the way back a boy comes towards them and says they must go home. The youngest child is ill. When they get home the child is dead.
16847: It is said of Piter de Graaf, who lives in Pein, that he was born with a caul. He can predict when someone will die. He is always right.
16848: A baker often has a new journeyman. The journeymen always meet their end in a strange way. A new journeyman arrives, a strong young fellow. He has to bake alone at night right away. The door opens and seven cats come in; they sit at the end of the kneading trough and want to throw him into it. The journeyman beats them to it and throws boiling water over the cats. The next morning the cats are dead. No journeyman ever died again.
16850: Tseard Kuipers, the narrator's father-in-law, fancies some apples. With a friend he goes to Rikele Myt's yard. They each have a sack with them. The sacks fill up. They want to leave. They cannot possibly get off the yard. In the end they have to empty the sacks. Rikele Myt caused this; she can do magic.
16851: Two people live in Twizelerheide. Their little daughter is ill. The man says to his wife: "We won't keep our girl, there goes the funeral." On the path is a drake with 7 ducks. A week later is the child's funeral. The hearse in front and 7 people behind it.
16852: Rapke Tuinstra and his brother-in-law Beam Reisma go out to catch moles. When they are near Gjert Oosterwoud in the Wylgen, Rapke says that Beam is pushing him into the ditch. Beam denies it. Splash. Rapke is in the ditch. According to Rapke he was cycling in the middle of the road. It was as if he was pulled into the canal along a line. He had collided with a funeral procession.
16854: This story is about Wibe Alma. When he is drunk he wants to fight, even with the devil. At closing time the innkeeper puts him out the door, as the police may come at any moment. In the street stands a small little man. He grabs Wibe and throws him into the Langewyk. With great effort he climbs out and has then come to his senses. That little man was the devil.
16855: The story is about a man who, when drunk, smashes everything in the house to pieces. His wife then takes refuge with the neighbours. When she returns, her husband lies asleep under the table. One time it happens again. As the woman slips off to the neighbours, she sees a little dog go into the house. When she comes home again the little dog is gone and the man lies in front of the house. The little dog had got hold of him; that was the devil himself.
16857: Edzer Sint can make little soldiers come out of a hearth pit. It sometimes happens that he needs money and cannot pay, but the next day he has a lot of money. He has a wisseldaalder (a magic coin that always returns to its owner).
16859: Fire as a harbinger of a fire. Some time later such a house then burns down.
16867: Two white women haunt the Lytse Wei. People do not go past there in the dark.
16868: A man cycles along the Lytse Wei in the evening. For no reason he is pushed from one side of the road to the other.
16869: A woman goes with a friend to the singing evening of the Salvation Army. On the way home one ends up in the ditch and the other against the house. It is a funeral procession that pushed her aside. Shortly afterwards her mother dies.
16870: Lanterns out in the open are the forerunners of other lanterns (on bicycles and the highway).
16875: A man from Harkema is out polecat hunting. It is Saturday night, close to midnight. He sees a light burning in a cottage. People are standing there peering in. When he comes closer, there is a foal with its forelegs on the windowsill, watching what is happening inside. The man gets scared and runs off.
16877: A woman who sold milk and butter fell ill and died. When she had been dead for a while, the children saw their mother again. Later the father and the housekeeper saw her too. The housekeeper asked her where she came from. Then the woman said she still owed a debt to people to whom she had not delivered milk and butter. The housekeeper paid those people back and the woman was never seen again.
16880: A man was walking on a road with some young people. Then he saw a funeral procession coming and could make out everything clearly. Later a real funeral procession came past at that same place. It was all the same, except there was one horse and cart fewer. But a little later they came along too and the procession was complete.
16885: Jetse van der Veen was visiting his friend Aen van der Wey. Suddenly he saw a very fat black sheep running. They did not know whose it was and went after it. The sheep began to dance. They could not catch it. It was too quick for them every time. Suddenly Alle Tet stood before them and said: "Oh, oh, how nicely I made you run, didn't I?"
16889: Some people in Harkema went to the black mirror. In it they could see whom they would marry. If no man or woman could be seen in it, it was a coffin. That meant the person would not marry.
16891: Alle Tet changed into a cat now and then. If someone gave the cat a thrashing, Tet was black and blue shortly afterwards.
16892: The narrator's father and brother were once threshing. A very fat cat was sitting in the back of the house. They kept an eye on the cat, because they suspected who it was. When his brother hit the cat with the pitchfork, it seemed to be dead. They went to drink coffee and were going to bury it afterwards. But when the time came, the cat was gone. The next day the old woman they had in mind was black and blue.
16893: A minister had to visit a woman. She was said to be a witch, but the minister wanted to be sure. She never came to church. She started baking pancakes for him. When she had three ready, she brought them to him and went back to baking. He did not eat them but quickly wrapped them in a newspaper and a cloth. When she came back in, he said he urgently had to leave and would come back another time. At home he put the pancakes in a pan with a lid on it. The next day there were three toads in the pan.
16894: You must never accept currant buns from a witch; they are bewitched.
16895: The maid on a farm has a sweetheart. When her fiancé comes to visit, the farmer's wife is able to tell her the next day what she and her boyfriend talked about. One time her boyfriend is there again and a fat strange cat lies purring. The cat will not be chased away. The next morning the farmer comes to say that his wife is unwell. He has to go out, but the maid is not allowed to go to the farmer's wife. The maid goes in to look and sees the farmer's wife lying in bed purple and blue. The maid understands. The farmer's wife is a witch.
16896: A friend of Harm Schievink lives with his grandmother in de Ham. Grandma has a large doll. When nobody is home, she is busy with it. One time the boys are peeping in; grandma takes the doll and forcefully sticks pins into it. They leave and come back later. Grandma is still sticking pins into the doll. Harm coughs loudly. In no time the old woman has put the doll things away.
16903: A man from the Wâlden travels by chaise to Ljouwert. Near Swarteweisein there is a farm where three men are threshing in the barn. At the barn the horse rears. The man whips it, but the horse will not take another step. The three men in the barn stand laughing. The man repeatedly asks who has done this to him. The men laugh even harder. The man goes and kicks a spoke out of one of the wheels. At that very moment one of the three men drops dead. He has broken his neck.
16906: Ruerd van der Veen is a carpenter in Hamsterheide; his nickname is Mike Ruerd. An odd fellow who cares about nothing. He wants nothing more than to see the devil once in the shape of a beautiful woman. He works in the Bomkleaster. When he goes home in the evening he has to cross the fields, over planks laid across the ditches. On one of those planks a woman blocks his way. He warns her to get out of the way or he will beat her to death, and reaches for his toolbox. The woman grabs him and hurls him into the field. When Ruerd gets up and tries to grab her, she throws him down with such force that he loses consciousness. The next day he came home lame. His wife and daughter fetched the tools.
16908: A man can cure warts, make little soldiers come out of the hearth pit, cut a black thread into short pieces and make it whole again, or turn a black thread red, white or blue.
16928: A man has worked in the city and earned a lot of money. He gets thoroughly drunk and curses and swears. On the way home he is grabbed by the shoulder and flung away. He still has a mark from it on his shoulder.
16929: A man always has money at hand. Boys sometimes get something from him. When he runs out, he has money again the next day. He has a wisseldaalder (a coin that always returns).
16930: Whoever wants a wisseldaalder (a coin that always returns) must walk around the church three times with a cat in a sack and each time call at the church door: 'Who will buy my cat for a daalder?' The third time he hands the sack to someone standing behind the door and receives a daalder in exchange.
16939: A man had seen the mill in Harkema on fire some time before it really burnt down.
16940: The narrator saw his neighbour's farm burn down three weeks before it really burnt down.
16955: The great church of Alkmaar is built on ox hides.
16957: A witch has made a child ill by sorcery. She can change into a cat. Once when her cat had been beaten, the witch had a bruise under her eye the next day.
16958: In his youth, the narrator's family always wore asafoetida (devil's dung) on their chests and their shirts back to front against witchcraft. They did not dare go to Alle Tet, the witch, to buy pot lids. The witch once told his mother that she had been to Spain in the night, drunk wine and flown back on her broom.
16959: If the magpies chatter, visitors are coming; if the magpies are silent, a death is coming. If the dog howls eerily, a death is coming. In the past, when the Hamster clock stopped, a death always followed too.
16963: A witch has dolls. When she sticks a needle into one, the person she has it in for feels pain.
16966: People saw an inn on fire long before it burnt down.
16967: At the place where a house was later built, people had earlier seen a light burning.
16968: A man can see in advance what is going to happen. He goes to places where a funeral will come.
16970: A man drives a bread cart. Once he is troubled by a plaagbeest (tormenting beast). When he gives it a piece of bread, it pulls his cart a long way.
16972: Wild lanterns are omens of later houses and lights along the road.
16974: Nightmares squeeze a person's throat shut. One of seven girls is a nightmare. She always comes through the keyhole. Remedies against the nightmare are scattering flour (they may not take it with them) and putting one slipper the right way and the other backwards in front of the bed.
16980: A wisseldaalder is a rijksdaalder with magic power. Whoever has one and spends it always gets it back in his purse. To get one you must sell yourself to the devil.
16981: A ventriloquist was once seen entering the town through all seven gates at the same moment. He can also make the cattle in the stable dance.
16987: A young farmhand sleeps in a box bed with another farmhand. At night the latter lies sweating in bed. The next morning he tells the boy that when he takes the horses to the field, the horses will stand with their heads towards him. That morning the reins are completely knotted and the horses stand backwards in front of the wagon. The farmer and a labourer come along. The labourer says that he and the farmhand had spread manure until it was time to go home. The rest of the manure had then flown apart by itself. When the farmer hears this, he drives the farmhand away.
16990: The narrator's brother used to be friends with the sons of a witch. Sometimes the witch gives him a thin slice of rye bread thickly spread with lard because she thinks he looks so poorly. One time, afterwards, his eight young ruffs fly around inside his house at home; another time he gets terrible pains and vomits up lots of live sticklebacks.
16991: If you want to send a jack of spades out for a bottle of liquor, you put two cards in a tin, curse the Supreme Being and write something on the tin. Someone puts the tin round the corner of the door. A little later the devil is standing there with a bottle of liquor, and the person who put the tin outside takes it from him. These are real devil's arts.
16998: A barn is haunted. In a certain spot in the barn no one can sleep. Whoever does is lifted up and thrown a long way off. Someone is said to have hanged himself there once.
17009: The narrator's mother sees a bright lamp burning above the canal. Later a bridge was built there with a lamp above it.
17012: Every morning a purse of money hangs on a woman's door. It is brought during the night. But it is devil's money: the woman has sold her soul to the devil.
17013: A woman has a wisseldaalder (a coin that always returns). She is a Freemason.
17017:
The narrator once meets a very tall woman, dressed entirely in black. When he greets her, she does not greet him back. When he looks away for a moment, she is suddenly gone.
(He also once had such an encounter at another place.)
17018: The narrator is walking beside a man born with a caul. The man pulls him aside when a funeral procession passes. The narrator does not see the procession.
17019: A wizard gives two poor farmhands a rijksdaalder (two-and-a-half-guilder coin) so they can have a drink in the café. When the farmhands want to pay, the rijksdaalder turns out to be a slice of carrot.
17020: A wizard goes to the market and asks a market woman how much her eggs cost. The wizard buys one egg, smashes it, and gold coins come rolling out. The market woman then refuses to sell the rest of her eggs. She smashes them all herself, but not a single gold coin comes out.
17021: A wizard is arrested and banished from the town: he must have left the town before midnight. The town has four gates. At midnight the wizard is seen leaving through all four gates.
17027: A naked little child that haunts the undergrowth no longer appears after the Lord's Prayer has been said.
17030: A certain woman always foresees deaths.
17031: A certain woman always foresees the arrival of visitors a day in advance.
17038: A group is riding along the road on two bicycles. Two of them see an enormous dog with eyes as big as saucers, but the other two see nothing.
17039: A man with a horse and cart is followed by a strange, ghostly, brightly coloured bird.
17040: A Freemason receives a wisseldaalder (a coin that always returns) from the devil. When changing it, however, the Freemason must always keep some money back, even if only a cent.
17045: Ale van Marten in Oudega was born with a caul. She saw funerals in advance. Once she saw a funeral procession coming across the land, which was still water then. A while later a daughter of Hindrik de Vries died. Those people lived in the polder and had to cross the water, otherwise they could not reach the road. The body had to be taken by boat across the water to the churchyard. Ale had seen all of that in advance.
17046: Before the narrator was married, he worked as a dairy hand in Germany. There was also an Italian there. He could do all sorts of things. He simply turned beer into water and could lift a large cask full of water between his thumb and finger. He sent the farmer to the stable to clear away dung, and the farmer obeyed like a little dog. He could simply make someone stand so that he could move neither forward nor backward.
17053: In the lane by Hattum de Vries a wit wijf (white woman) always haunted at night. People did not dare go there at night, because the white woman drove them to the side towards the little lake. Without doing anything themselves, they ended up in the lake.
17056: A nightmare was a woman who had to torment other people. She usually came through the keyhole. As protection, asafoetida was put under the threshold and the slippers were put upside down in front of the bed.
17057: In Oudega a foal with a porridge pot around its neck used to haunt the place.
17061: Jan Bruining was a cattle dealer in Opeinde. He was courting the daughter of Jelle Tryn. Once, on his way to her, he was seized and flung over the trees. That was the work of the devil. Jan Bruining was a very odd one. He did not much care what he did.
17062: A certain Houwink was once walking from Garijp to Oudega. Past a small bridge a man was walking ahead of him. He called to him a few times to wait. When the other said nothing back, he shouted angrily: "wait, devil!" Then the other stopped and slowly came closer and closer to him, so close that Houwink had to step aside right to the edge of the ditch. In the end he grabbed Houwink and hurled him over the bank. H. scrambled to his feet and said: "you did that, filthy devil!" Then the devil flung him much further still. From then on H. could no longer walk, so badly were his bones and back injured.
17071: The old church in Oudega is built on ox hides.
17074: The narrator's father had a cousin, Tseard de Wal. He was born with a caul. He knew everything in advance and saw beforehand that someone would die. When someone was ill, he could sometimes say: "I've already seen him as a corpse." Then you could be sure that person would not recover.
17075: Near the Skilige Piip a foal with a porridge pot around its neck ran about.
17077: One morning an old man on the Wal said: "Last night I gave a tomcat a wallop. It was prowling around the house. And now I know what it is. Did you see Antsje this morning with a red handkerchief around her neck? Well, then I don't need to say anything more."
17082: A certain Douwe lived on de Wal. He was always in the pub and was afraid of no one. He played curses on the accordion. But then the devil got hold of him one time. He was lifted up and flung over the trees. That was on the Priester-akker. Jehannes Procee was coming back from the women that night and walked along with him. Jehannes did not see the evil one. He was invisible. But Douwe lay on the ground foaming at the mouth. He never played again and became a faithful churchgoer.
17083: Someone else was once flung away on de Wal; he got back up and ran home so fast that he came into the hallway through the closed door.
17090: A man from Kollum wants to leave his girlfriend's in Zwagerbos towards morning. When he gets outside, he stands still for a while. Then he warns that a funeral procession will soon come past from a house further along. Someone in the procession will wear a hat with a white plume. And so it came to pass.
17091: The narrator's father always said you should not walk in the middle of the road but always at the side, because a funeral procession may come along the road and then you get pushed aside.
17092: A man from Kollum was born with a caul. Once, when he is standing at the window with his father, he asks him to step aside. Later he explains that his child is going to die. He has seen people come in and set a coffin down in the room. A few days later the child has died, and the coffin is put down in the same spot where he had already seen it.
17094: The narrator's father is chopping chicory with a few others. Suddenly one of them stops and stares fixedly at the road. Then he says he has seen two funeral processions coming one after the other, and that the dead are related to each other. Shortly afterwards a brother and a sister die in Zwagerbos. They are buried in the churchyard at Kollumerzwaag. The procession passes the spot where they were working.
17095: One evening the narrator's father comes home with the cart and two young horses in front of it. At the spot where the railway now runs, he and his father suddenly hear a hellish noise. The horses become agitated and break out in a sweat. Shortly afterwards the railway is built there, and they hear the same sound when the train runs over the rails.
17096: Stammerige Harm is said to be able to work magic. He threatens children that he will make a crow come out of the hearth if they are naughty. They say he sometimes makes little soldiers come out of the hearth pit and march.
17097: A big black dog always runs past a woman's house in Zwagerbos. It is a plaagbeest (tormenting beast). When she says 'plaagbeest' it comes to her; when she says 'best beest' (good beast) it disappears again.
17098: The father was always troubled by a nightmare at night. From the moment the woman suspected of it died, the nightmare no longer came. She was one of seven sisters.
17099: A werewolf is a fellow just like us. One evening the narrator is at a Saint Nicholas raffle in Tsjerkebos. Suddenly a young man bites him in the shoulder. When he asks him why he is biting, the man neighs like a horse. The next day there are large tooth marks in his skin. The young man is one of seven brothers.
17103: Three farmhands sleep in a farmer's barn. At night cats come into the barn and make a lot of noise. One night one of them, the youngest, the boy who milks the sheep, keeps watch with a pitchfork. When the cats come in and start making noise, he throws the pitchfork at them. One of the cats is hit. The next day the farmhands are woken by the farmer's wife instead of the farmer. The farmer has trouble with his shoulder. It was the farmer who was hit by the pitchfork. He is a sorcerer.
17106: The brother of a woman who has died had already seen the whole funeral beforehand. He was pushed aside when the funeral procession went past.
17112: Uncle Piter in Suameerderheide saw someone make little soldiers come out of the hearth.
17115: Against nightmares one must scatter flour on the floor.
17122: A man has seen a house on fire, but it has not burnt down yet.
17123: Many people saw the lights of the tram long before it ran.
17124: On the path from Suameerderheide to De Harste lies a foal with a porridge pot around its neck.
17125: The narrator's father walks a girl home at night. On the way a dog as big as a calf comes past. It is a plaagbeest (tormenting beast).
17130: The soldiers with whom the narrator's father is serving want to send a jack of spades out for a bottle of liquor. The one who has to take the bottle is scared to death. When the bottle has been taken, they pour out a glassful and fling the glass empty over their shoulder with the words: 'that is for you'. That is the devil. Then they drink the bottle empty together.
17132: Jehannes van der Zee is a dissolute man. Once, on the Harstelaan, he is terribly beaten and flung about by the devil. Later he changed his ways and never went to that spot again.
17134: A foal with a porridge pot around its neck walks on the Langewyk.
17162: The narrator's uncle is once coming back from work. A fellow is walking ahead of him. He asks him to wait, but the man gives no answer. When his uncle threatens to bash his brains in, the fellow grabs him and flings him over the trees, twice over.
17165: A man is troubled by the devil. On the way home he talks without stopping until he is home. That is a protection against the devil. At home the man is beaten by the devil. His wife then has to sing psalms to drive the devil away.
17335: During the German occupation a boy from the narrator's family is arrested and transported to Germany. Before he comes home quite unexpectedly, the narrator's father has already seen the boy arriving.
17336: One evening the narrator's wife sees a funeral procession approaching. She goes to put salt in the potatoes, but when she comes back the procession has vanished. Shortly afterwards a funeral notice arrives and an old housekeeper of hers is buried. She does not know whether it is the same funeral she had already seen.
17339: A man always has to get up at night when a funeral procession is coming. He cannot help it. He has to see it.
17340: One evening the narrator is out with his father. Suddenly his father says they must stand beside the path for a moment. His father does not say he sees a funeral procession, but he does see it.
17341: Whoever joins the Freemasons sells himself to the devil. He then gets as much money as he wants and also has a wisseldaalder (a coin that always returns).
17353: The wild lanterns of the past were the forerunners of the bicycle.
17361: In a cottage by a big tree lives an old man who can work magic. In the evening a few cats always run around the tree, singing and dancing all the while. When they are chased off, they come back. They hold meetings under the tree. They are witches.
17363: Witches always work with currant buns. The buns they give turn into toads.
17364: A witch gives an old woman an apple. The woman puts the apple under a bowl on a cupboard. The next day the apple has turned into a toad.
17367: Freemasons curse everything. The devil gains power over them. A Freemason in Veenklooster met a strange end. Freemasons have a wisseldaalder (a coin that always returns). Stuttering Harm is a Freemason too. When he is short of money, he hangs an empty sack on the door, and in the morning it is full again.
17368: When a dog howls eerily, it sees a funeral procession. Then people say: 'there's another one lying at death's door'.
17374: At night a big black dog lurks on the Wildpad, and when someone has to cycle past, it sometimes rests its head on the bicycle's mudguard for a long while. It is a plaagbeest (tormenting beast).
17375: The narrator and his wife saw lights near the churchyard in the evening. Later, street lighting came there.
17376: The narrator and his wife sometimes see lights low to the ground along the canal near Surhuisterveen in the evening. People say a motorway will come there. The light sometimes crosses the canal too, so a bridge would also have to come. Some also say they are the lights of a train.
17378: A man always goes to the farmer at four in the morning. He has to pass through a wood. There a handful of cats often gather to hold a meeting. The witch Alle Tet is among them as a cat.
17379: Near the narrator's parents-in-law, the house where they used to lodge is on fire. Piter Schievink had already seen it on fire beforehand.
17380: In his youth a man was once flung across the Lange Wyk by the devil.
17381: The grandfather and father of the narrator's wife are as wicked as the devil. The grandfather is once on his way home after a carpentry job. Suddenly a woman in long skirts is standing on a pile of wood. He greets her three times, but she says nothing back. He gets angry and curses: 'now you'll say something, even if you are the devil'. Then the woman picks him up and flings him away. He is ill from it for a week.
17382: The grandfather of the narrator's wife treats his wife badly. He sometimes throws her into the dung pit full of water, muck and mud, and when she climbs out he kicks her back in. He can work magic; he can bend tea saucers and make little soldiers come out of the hearth pit. He puts those little soldiers to work, or else they will go after him. He has them separate milk and water. They cannot do it. The man also has a book of magic. He cannot get rid of it. If he burns it, it comes back. But when, on someone's advice, he sells it at half the price, he is rid of it.
17383: An old man sometimes comes to chat with the grandfather of the narrator's wife in the evening. When there is a knock at the door, the grandfather has to go outside for a moment. Then he gets such a beating that he cries out. That is the devil settling accounts with him.
17385: A woman has a vision of a girl in a red apron drowning in a pond. Shortly afterwards the narrator's thirteen-year-old sister drowns in the pond when she falls through the ice while skating. She is wearing a red apron.
17386: The narrator's cousin once goes from Surhuisterveen back to De Harkema along the road that funeral processions take to the churchyard. Three times he is pushed off the road. Finally he is thrown into a ditch. This was done by a funeral procession he was walking in the way of.
17387: A man who does not take life too seriously is once drinking and cursing in the pub and says he feels like fighting, even if it were with the devil. He is barely outside when someone comes along who keeps walking closer and closer to him. The man gets very frightened and breaks into a run. But the other keeps running close beside him. It is the devil. He comes home white as a sheet and it is a miracle he survived. He repented at once, never cursed again and has gone to church on Sundays ever since.
17394: To ward off a nightmare one must scatter flour in front of the bed, or say the Our Father. A man once scattered flour in front of his bed in the stable at the farm where he slept. The nightmare stepped into it and then could not get away. The next morning she was sitting behind the winnowing machine in the barn.
17395: A man was born with a caul. He sees everything in advance. He also saw in advance the house where the narrator's mother-in-law and her family lived burn down.
17399: A wizard uses a formula to spoil a conjurer's show (making the tricks visible), to the latter's fury.
17410: Two boys are given shelter by a farmer in a haunted house. They are warned that they may only answer if the farmer asks them something. A little later the farmer asks whether the boys want porridge. They do not dare answer, and a voice says: the farmer is asking you something. Then they answer. Next the voice sounds again, asking whether they want more. Without thinking, the boys immediately answered: yes. Then they are beaten by the ghost and they flee.
17445: Someone puts a bottle of gin around the corner of the door with a jack of spades beside it. When the bottle later comes floating into the room, that person becomes very frightened, because whoever put the bottle there may never take hold of it. He asks someone else to take the bottle, and the first glass of gin is thrown over the right shoulder.
17446: Edzer Sint can make soldiers come out of a stoke hole.
17447: Behind Ljouwert lived an old woman who could do magic. A man comes by one evening to talk with her, but she is in a deep sleep all evening, so the man talks with her husband. When the man has finished talking and goes home, he tells his wife that the old woman slept all evening. His wife expresses her astonishment, because the old woman was with her all evening drinking coffee and talking. Then the man is convinced that the woman is a witch and decides never to visit her again. In the chair lies a tripe, which he had taken for the woman. But when they hear the outer door slam, they know for certain that the woman is a witch.
17448: When Bauke Schievink goes home, the devil is with him. When he comes out of the pub, too, he often gets lashed with a whip by the devil. Bauke's daughter is called Metsje and is a card reader.
17455: One night, while her husband is not home, a woman sees a coffin being carried into the house. The coffin is too small for the man and the woman and too large for the children. When she tells her husband the story, he no longer wants to live in the house and the family moves. Another family comes to live in the house; the sons are in poor health. One day one of the boys dies, and he fits exactly in the coffin the previous occupant had seen back then.
17459: If you want a magic coin, you must run around the churchyard three times with a cat in a sack and say three times 'Who will buy my cat for a daalder?'. Then you get a magic coin.
17467: Two men work in Germany. There is a fair and the men go to a fortune teller in a tent with a black mirror. They are each shown a card with a picture of their future wife. They must leave the tent walking backwards. In the magic mirror they also see their future wives. Later both men marry the woman they saw in the mirror.
17469: It is late and someone sees through the window a funeral procession on its way to the churchyard. But there is no deceased with it. That night old Gradus dies, and at his funeral everything looks exactly the same.
17473: It is summer and twelve men are lying in the sand. It is around half past one at night when they hear the sound of hammers further on. When they go to look, the sound stops. This happens three times. Some three or four years later the new Reformed church would come to stand on that spot.
17474: A father is on his way home at night with some other people. In the distance they see a group of people approaching and they hide for fear of being robbed. A solemn procession passes. The last man wears a tailcoat and briefly looks at the father. The father thinks it was a funeral procession.
17479: A young man is walking on the road at night and it is dead quiet. Suddenly there are people all around him. They run past him without saying anything. When someone is buried later, he realises he has seen the funeral procession.
17484: Around 1910 a woman went door to door with wares. She sees a place in Sânbulten ablaze. But when she runs over to it, there is no trace of fire.
17488: In the past witte wieven (white women) were often seen at night in Westerein.
17489: Someone used to see wild lanterns often. When bicycles and cars later made their appearance, people said those lanterns had of course been the lights of the bicycles and cars.
17493: There was an old man who often had to get out of bed at night to go and look at something. If he stayed in bed, he was more or less thrown out of it. He often went to the churchyard, and once he saw a funeral procession there.
17494: Harke Woudwyk lived with his sister Gels in Westerein. He could make little soldiers come out of the stoke hole and dance on the table.
17498: Someone once heard psalm singing in the air. That was the forerunner of the radio.
17499: Someone sees a fire as an omen. Later the house really does burn down.
17500: When the magpie chatters, something bad is about to happen. When the bird flies against the glass, a death is imminent.
17505: Jehannes (Hindrikje) could fix people in place so that they could no longer move from the spot.
17521: A man is gathering food for his sheep when he sees a brown beast spinning round and round fast. It is a kind of big dog, and the man is so frightened that he leaves the bag of food and runs home. The man thinks it is the same phantom dog that got hold of Doctor Wiegersma.
17525: Someone can make soldiers come out of the stoke hole. This story is also used to frighten children.
17529: Among the Freemasons someone must die every seven years. They draw lots for it. Because they have no money, the Freemasons hang up a boot without a sole. The devil then puts money in it. Some of them have also had a wisseldaalder (a coin that always returns) from the devil. With a cat on their arm they call up the devil. Sometimes the devil is tricked with the words 'Who will buy my hare for a daalder?'. The devil later finds he has bought a cat in a sack. So the Freemasons never lack money.
17532: A little pig runs about on the Veen at night. Everyone avoids the place, because it is a phantom animal.
17533: Bauke Schievink is out walking and is startled by the devil at his side. The devil stays at his heels and keeps baring his teeth. A passing minister sees the pair walking and thinks Bauke keeps rather shady company. At a small wood the devil suddenly disappears.
17534: A boy wants to fight a ghost dog, but he cannot get the better of it in the fight. The dog is the devil.
17536: As a girl, a woman was much troubled by nightmares. Her mother advised her to shout very loudly three times 'Devil, devil, you will not master me' when the nightmare tormented her again. After that the girl was never troubled by nightmares again.
17539: A cyclist is often grabbed on the bridge by an invisible ghost.
17541: A man always carries on terribly. When, cursing, he claims he is not afraid of the devil, the devil appears to him. The devil strikes him down so hard that the house shakes on its foundations.
17542: Witte wieven (white women) mostly haunt on wooden planks.
17545: A pig and a foal often run about with a porridge pot around their necks. They are phantom animals. A glowing man also walks about. He is the devil.
17548: Near a small labourer's cottage a man suddenly sees a little coffin standing in the street. Later the people who live there lose their child.
17549: Three men are running side by side in the meadow when suddenly the one in the middle is lifted up and set aside. A little later a funeral procession passes, which none of the three can see.
17550: In the past you could often see wild lanterns. Those will-o'-the-wisps were the omens of car and bicycle lights.
17551: A family lives in a detached house. When the son once comes home in the middle of the night, he hears sounds of hammering. He tells his father that a new house will be built. A year later the house is indeed there.
17553: Ruerd van der Veen could make soldiers come out of the stoke hole and march through the house. Ruerd was also a carpenter. Once, when the road was blocked by wood, a woman grabbed him and flung him over the woodpile. Then Ruerd was almost home.
17554: A number of men are playing cards and want a bottle of drink. One of them ties a jack of spades to an empty bottle and sends the bottle away. A little later the bottle comes floating into the room, filled. The man who sent the bottle away does not dare take hold of it, because that would be his death. Then someone else takes it. The first glass of gin is thrown over the shoulder; the second is drunk.
17557: A horse's head haunts the place between the Reformed and the Dutch Reformed church.
17562: A farmer has one grain bay in which nothing will ever grow. He always warns people not to sleep in the gap. One man ignores his warnings and makes his bed there. In the middle of the night he is suddenly thrown roughly out of the grain bay.
17564: A man sees a funeral procession going by and becomes very frightened. It is an omen.
17579:
If a dog howls eerily, someone will die. Before the death of a boy, a dog howled for three nights. When he had died, the howling stopped.
A woman heard the neighbours' dog howling eerily. The next day her own son died.
17580: A father-in-law and his family once hear a thud in the house. Outside there is nothing to be seen. But the next day, when a thatcher falls off the roof, they hear exactly the same thud for real.
17581: A woman claimed to see all sorts of things. At night she often got out of bed and then she saw funeral processions.
17582: A girl was often tied up and beaten by her father. Once, when she had again been mistreated like this, a little man in a tailcoat, wearing a small hat and with a stick under his arm, climbed the ladder to the loft. Things got so terrible there that the whole house trembled and shook. It was the devil punishing the father in this way. Fourteen days later the daughter died.
17583: A pottery peddler carried his wares in a cart pulled by two dogs. When they passed a place where the devil lived, the dogs refused to pull any further. The man then had to pull the cart himself until they were past that place.
17584:
In the evening a dog, with its paws on the windowsill, looks in at a man and his family. So the man goes to a devil banisher. He tells him he has come too late. Not long afterwards his child dies. In the dead child's pillow the family finds wreaths with all sorts of little rags wound around them. The rags are of the same fabric as the clothes the child wore on the day it died.
If the man had come to the devil banisher sooner, the child would have lived.
17585:
A big, rugged man is going home after a day of carpentry. He takes the back way, over the little wooden bridge, when someone comes walking beside him. Suddenly he is hurled over the tree trunks. The next day his daughter fetches his toolbox.
He then had to stay in bed for a full three weeks.
17588: The will-o'-the-wisps that used to be seen here were omens of the lamps. People later got much more light.
17589: A man was always much troubled by nightmares (mares). He saw the nightmare coming. The nightmare climbed from his feet higher and higher and in the end squeezed his throat shut. The man said he had never seen the nightmare.
17590: One evening a man's wagon is followed by a beast. The man kneels down to see better what kind of beast it is. The beast is very big and yellow, and it flaps its ears. It passes right by the man and stays with him for a while. The man thinks it was a plaagbeest (tormenting beast).
17592: A man sent jacks of spades to fetch bottles of drink. His wife practised kaartleggen (fortune-telling with cards). Another woman who practised kaartleggen (fortune-telling with cards) always carried cards in her blouse.
17593: Close to a very small house was a pool from which some people now and then very clearly heard cries of "Help, help!" People thought they were ghostly sounds. The mothers always warned the children: "Don't come too near the pool, for someone will drown there one day."
17594: Foppe Sint had a magic coin and it was said of him that he had sold himself to the devil. He did not speak properly. Once, when he was about to sit down, his little daughter quickly pulled the chair away behind him. He fell backwards onto the floor. He said to his wife: "Oh dear, my head is as tangled as a tree root."
17595: The wood in the Hamsterheide is haunted. The Achterwei is haunted too. There is always a little fellow sitting on a ladder there.
17596: Mike Ruerd was hurled down by Satan. The devil has got hold of him for good. Another man was hurled down too. He was strange and drank far too much.
17599: Will-o'-the-wisps could often be seen at the Fjouwer Roeden. If you were thinking about them in the dark, you saw them. Hindriks Lol said that will-o'-the-wisps were signs of new houses. And indeed new houses soon appeared.
17600: A neighbour comes to tell a mother that her little son has drowned in a pool. When the mother tells her aunt about it right afterwards, the aunt says she already knew. The aunt tells her that the neighbour has just been to tell her too.
17601: All the little paths of Smoarhoeke in Harkema are haunted.
17602: If you are troubled by a nightmare (a mare), you must lay a wet floorcloth in front of the bed.
17606: A farmer had a very vicious farm dog. After some bargaining, Jehannes Tsyske bought the dog from the farmer. The dog, which everyone was afraid of, ran after Jehannes to his house like a puppy.
17613: A skipper's vessel was untied time and again by a little boy and a little girl. The skipper went to the minister and explained the matter to him. The minister wanted to know more and asked the children why they did it. The children said they had been murdered at that spot and had never been given grave clothes. Then the minister had to promise that they would get burial clothes. To do so, he had to stop the very first woman he met. This woman had to buy the cloth. The minister did as he had been asked and brought the grave clothes to the skipper. He laid the parcel on the deck. The boy and the girl took it from there, and after that the skipper was never untied again.
17617: A household of four people was going to move. Jehannes predicted that only three of them would leave. The man died before the move.
17619: If a card was sent out to get a bottle of drink, the person who was to receive the bottle had to be very steadfast indeed. The one who sends the card must on no account receive the bottle.
17627: There are sorceresses who stick large pins into dolls. Their victims then suffer for it.
17630: A nightmare (a mare) is one of seven daughters, but it is sometimes an only daughter. You can hear her when she comes running on tiptoe. Then she comes beside you and a moment later she is sitting on your neck. You cannot sneeze then. If you swear her away, she never comes again. Sprinkling rye helps. Or putting rye bread on the bed board.
17632: A black dog haunts the area between Blauwhuis and the Boelenslaan.
17635: On the Feanster Heide a man heard something scraping against the window frame one night. When he saw nothing outside, he went back to bed. A little later something wooden was set down outside and something was thrown on top of it. Again the man went to look, but again he saw nothing. Two weeks later his son died. When the coffin was carried out of the house, it scraped against the frame. It was the same sound as fourteen days before. At the churchyard, where the bier was set down and the carrying poles thrown on top of it, the father heard the other sounds. The time between the sounds was the same as on that night.
17636: People saw two girls wearing little red aprons at the edge of the Blaudobbe in Houtigehage. The people feared it meant a haunting, because in reality those girls were not there. People no longer let their children go too near the Blaudobbe.
17637: At a farm that stood crosswise to the road, things were not right. Every night two ghosts wandered there, whom the farmer greatly disliked. His neighbour, who was no speaker himself, advised him to fetch a minister. The minister was to ask the ghosts what they wanted. The farmer went from minister to minister, but none would help him. At last, in a small out-of-the-way village, he found a willing minister. He came along and asked for a red handkerchief. He folded it diagonally and held it in his right hand. The ghosts then told the minister that they were father and son and had lived at this place. They had died suddenly and still had a great deal of money lying here. The money was in a secret compartment in one of the horizontal beams between the posts of the barn. As long as the money was not removed, they would find no rest. The farmer who lived there now was to get half the money, and the church the other half. The minister threw the handkerchief to the ghosts as a sign that their wish would be fulfilled. The handkerchief was completely scorched when the ghosts took it. With half the money the farmer could buy a piece of land he rented. And he still had money left over. And that was the end of the haunting.
17638: Around 1800 there was a girl who wished every day to see her dead mother. One evening she heard her mother's shuffling footsteps outside. The moment she saw her mother coming, she wished she were gone. The mother vanished again, and from then on the girl was at peace.
17639: Two men were out hunting polecats. All night they caught nothing. When they suddenly saw a very fine polecat, the frightened dogs would not seize it. One of the men then wanted to catch the animal himself. But the polecat sat on his neck and would not come off. The man walked home like that, and only when he had crossed the threshold did the animal let him go.
17644: A man left for America with his family. When he arrived there, he wrote to his relatives that on the way they had heard a mermaid singing. A mermaid is a creature, half woman, half fish. On board they said that this meant there was a dead person on board, or that one would come. Then his little child died on board. They lowered the little coffin into the sea.
17645: Minse Griper could make little soldiers come out of the hearth pit by reading aloud from a book of magic. Then he had the soldiers march. When he read the same thing backwards, the soldiers went back into the hearth pit. But once he could not do it quickly enough. He shouted to his wife to throw a sack of rye and oats into the back of the house. Then he had time to read backwards and get the soldiers back into the hearth pit. The rooks were there at once. They separated the rye and the oats.
17649: Around 1916, one evening, I saw very long, white, tall things standing against the sky. But I never knew what it was.
17650: A man heard every time at the same spot: "You will come to live here." He did not like that at all, because there was nothing but heath and wilderness at that spot. After five years the man moved to another house, but he still heard every time at that one spot that he would come to live there. He always heard it behind him, never in front of him. After four years he did indeed come to live there.
17651: Once a drunken man is sleeping in the woods. He was woken by the sound of hammering, but he saw nothing at all. Later 'de Huchte' was built on that very spot.
17652: A family used to see rows of wild lanterns on the Folgersterloane. It looked just like a number of wagons one behind the other. That was later the tram from Drachten to Grins.
17657: A woman was once coming back from Houtigehage when she saw a small child come out from under a big spruce tree. That child had been buried there in secret, so it found no rest.
17662: People often hear the sound of a small child coming from the Popkepoel at night. They think it is an omen, but so far no child has drowned.
17663: A boy takes part in a spiritualist séance. Suddenly he sees a coffin standing by the box bed. He looks away, but when he looks again, the coffin is still there. When he looks for the third time, the coffin is gone. A fortnight later the woman of the house dies and her coffin is placed in the same spot in front of the box bed.
17664: A boy often hears hammering at night. Later a house is built on that spot. It is an omen.
17667: A werewolf is a person who is half man and half woman.
17668: In the past many wild lanterns were seen. They were omens of the later street lamps.
17669: A married couple have special powers. The wife is a card reader; the husband can make bottles of drink float into the house. He sends an empty bottle away with a jack of spades and the bottle comes back filled. At first the man does not dare take hold of the bottle himself, and the bottle circles around the lamp for a while. When he finally takes the drink, he throws the first glass over his left shoulder. That is for the devil.
17670: A prisoner can simply escape through the closed doors of the prison.
17672: If the bell does not strike, a dead person is hanging from the clapper. If magpies flutter around the house, a death is imminent.
17674: In a mirror tent, men can see the image of their future wife in a black mirror. If they will not marry, they see a coffin.
17677:
Bloodstains from a murder cannot be washed away.
In some houses there is a hole that cannot be closed. The devil is in it.
17678: At a certain spot a fellow often runs around at night. It is a ghostly apparition.
17679: Nobody dares to sleep in a barn. It is a haunted place.
17680: A father and son see a ghostly apparition floating and take to their heels. This little story is very common and is told in many places.
17682: A boy is born with a caul and always foresees everything. Once, coming back from milking the cows, he sees a funeral procession. He is so frightened that he spills all the milk. His mother is very angry with him about the wasted milk. His father is not angry, because he sometimes sees omens himself.
17683: When a boy comes home from work at night, he sees that the windows of the house are open. When he goes inside, there is a small coffin on the floor. When his little sister's health starts to fail, he sees the little coffin again. Now it stands outside against the wall. When the sister dies, the little coffin stands inside in the same spot where the boy first saw it. When the body is carried out, he runs hard after it. The little coffin is placed in the same spot by the wall that he had seen.
17698: A boy tells his friend to step aside on the road. Later he says he saw a funeral procession go past.
17699: At a certain spot a white phantom horse always runs about. Everyone is afraid of it.
17700: A married couple are on their way home at night and hear a strange sound. It sounds as if a swarm of bees is passing through the trees. It is a haunted place.
17701: A shoemaker always hears sounds of hammering at night near the public school. Later two new houses were built there.
17702: It sometimes happened that people fancied a drink. Then they had to put a king of hearts in the hollow at the bottom of a bottle and go to the door with it backwards, because they were not allowed to see who took the bottle. Someone else then had to receive the full bottle, also backwards. The first dram then had to be thrown over the left shoulder. Everyone could then drink from the bottle, and it always stayed just as full.
17704: If the wreaths found in a pillow are burned, the sorceress is racked with pain. Some sorceresses stick pins into dolls. To keep sorceresses out, you must put asafoetida under the threshold of a door. Then the sorceresses cannot cross it.
17712: In Harkema lived a small man who sold coffins and smaller goods. He made little soldiers come out of the hearth pit. They drilled and marched around the room.
17713:
A man once went to the market. He was told: "If you want to know whom you will marry, you can get to see her." He went into the tent and saw a woman in a black mirror. She was a dark woman, and he later married her.
If you saw not a woman in the mirror but a coffin, you would not marry.
17715: A woman was running down the middle of the road. Then she thought: "Goodness, this is heavy going." Then she ended up sitting on a hearse.
17720: One night a man hears, close to the bridge, the noise of stones being loaded, hammering and tools being thrown about, and yet there was nothing to be seen. A short time later a construction factory was built there.
17721: One night a man hears hammering in his house without seeing anything. He could not understand what it was. Later the house was renovated.
17722: A boy came home one night. The windows had been pushed open and the curtains were flapping outwards. In the corner of the room he saw his youngest brother lying in a small coffin. That was witchcraft. The child was already ill at the time and died soon afterwards. The boy had said nothing to his mother, so as not to make her sad. But when the child was dead, he told her he had already known, because he had seen the little body in a coffin.
17723: An old man boarded with a married couple. At night he often got out of bed because he had to see hearses. As he grew older, it cost him more and more effort. He was then flung over hedges and fences by the devil just to be in time for the hearses. He was never late. When he really could not go on, he asked the couple to pray for him. The husband knew something about praying, and so the old man was released.
17724:
A woman wakes early in the morning and goes into the garden. When the neighbour girl asks why she is up so early, she says the magpies on the windowsill woke her. And that points to a death. The neighbour girl says: "The first one to come out the door will be the one, they say." The woman says she hopes it won't be her.
A little later the neighbour girl goes to her sister. Her sister's husband has forgotten his work trousers, and the girl takes them after him. She had already caught up with him when she tripped and fell flat on the street. She was dead on the spot.
17725: If a mirror falls and breaks into shards, there will be a death in the house or something else bad will happen.
17726: A dog stood howling eerily at the spot where a pram usually stands. The little child then died.
17731: One day the eldest farmhand said to the youngest farmhand: "How poorly you look, lad. How thin and weak you are." The youngest farmhand answered that he ate well enough, but that at night he always had to go out with the farmer's wife. He then has to say: "Over hills and over dales and over all the streams." All night long they travel through the air. She leaves her belly behind in bed with the farmer. The eldest farmhand offered to go out with the farmer's wife for a night, so the youngest could get some rest. But when the farmer's wife stood by the bed, the farmhand said the spell slightly differently; he did not say over hills, but through hills and through dales and through all the streams. Now it took almost a week before they came home again. All that time the woman's belly had lain in bed with the farmer. But the little woman had not enjoyed this journey. She had had enough of the night journeys for good. She was a nightmare.
17734: Some people who have a pact with the devil are bulletproof. Such people also have a magic coin. To get it, they must run around a church a few times with a cat and call through the door: "Cat sold! Cat sold!" Then a hand appears around the corner of the church door. It takes the cat and hands over the magic coin. They never lose the magic coin. When they spend it, they always get it back. So such people never run short of money.
17737: In the past there were many wild lanterns here. They were the forerunners of bicycles and buses.
17738: Near the Blauhûs there used to be a little bridge. A piebald watchdog always haunted it at night.
17741: The master of a state school once heard a voice from a pond say: "The place is here, the man is not." A short time later a pupil drowned in it.
17742: In Blaufallaet there were about thirteen houses, the last of which stood a little further back. Once a man rode past that old house at five to twelve. There he saw a very large dog. And suddenly the dog was gone again. But on one side there was a hedge, and on the other side water. Where had the dog gone? The place was uncanny and the man became frightened.
17744: Once when a man was out in the field, a very small brown dog floated past him. It headed for the canal. The man asked what the dog wanted, but the little creature disappeared into the water. Exactly three weeks later the same thing happened to the man's father. Then too the dog seemed to disappear into the canal. The place was uncanny.
17745: There was once a greedy man who even worked on Sundays. One time a very large black dog came and stood stock-still beside the man. The man could not and dared not go on working, because it was the devil in the shape of a dog. The man went home and never worked there again.
17747: A man scoffed that he could take on the devil. When he actually met the devil, he came out of the fight with broken clogs and torn clothes. A few days later he said he was ready for another encounter. After that time nothing he wore was still whole. Then he had had enough.
17748: In summer a man saw two very large bales of hay standing in the middle of the road. But nobody believed him. When he was cycling in the moonlight in autumn, he and his brother-in-law saw the bales again. But when they wanted to get closer, they suddenly disappeared. Nothing could be seen in the water either.
17749: A man and his sister were cycling on a moonlit, perfectly still evening when suddenly something struck the water. Three times the water splashed up very high.
17750: At an empty spot, people often heard hammering in the evening from nine o'clock on. Years later a farm came there.
17751: Near a canal people once heard hammering, but there was nothing to be seen. Two years later a wooden house was put up there.
17752: A black dog as big as a sheep haunted a sandy path near Surhuizum. A man claimed he was not afraid and said he would give that dog a kick. The following Sunday, around twelve o'clock, the dog was sitting in the middle of the cycle path. The man chased the dog for about 200 metres until it was gone.
17753: When a man hit his pregnant wife, she said she hoped God would put a mark on the child. One time the father and his hunchbacked little daughter were followed by a black dog. Once they got home, the dog even stayed sitting on the edge of his bed.
17754: A married couple hears sawing in the house one night. Later the house is completely renovated.
17916: Fairies can help you find something again. But they can also make you lose your way in the woods.
17923: A group of Wiccans goes out into nature to perform an initiation ritual. They neglect to ask the fairies for permission. This displeases the fairies, and they make the group lose their way.
18083: Jehannes Meerstra could make little soldiers come out of the hearth pit. Sometimes he made the sound of a crying child come out of the water. He could do ventriloquism.
18084: Two women once went to the market. A mirror foretold their future. One woman saw a man, whom she did indeed marry later. The other woman saw a coffin. She was told that in three weeks she would end up on the west side of the church. Within three weeks she died and was buried on the west side of the church.
18085: A man in a fairground tent was given a little portrait of a woman he would marry. He did indeed marry her.
18086: Even before railways were built, people heard the thunder of a train at that spot.
18087: Wild lanterns were the forerunners of bicycle lamps.
18088: A young man was harassed at night by a dog that was bigger than himself. When the man said he had nothing on his conscience, the plaagbeest (tormenting beast) went away again.
18091: Once a man and a woman were out walking when the woman (who had been born with a caul) said they had to get away from that spot. The man refused and held on to her. But suddenly she is sitting three metres further on, on the road. A hearse went past.
