38472: The bridge where the print of the devil's horse's hoof can still be seen is known as the devil's bridge.
38474: A man who meets a phantom funeral procession at night gets no answer to his greeting.
38486: Neighbours take turns keeping watch at night over a sick man and after his death. One of the neighbours sees him walking around the room at night, shouts that he is back, and runs off. Nobody knows what happened, but the neighbour is still told that he is back again.
38489: Of four women in the area who are witches, three can turn themselves into a cat. One night a local resident strikes a cat. The next morning the husband of one of the witches says that his wife has been beaten.
38490: A rhyme mentions a woman flying through the air on a broomstick.
38492: After the devil has come in the night, with the print of a horse's hoof as proof, a man who often plays cards burns the cards.
38493: The devil jumps over a canal. The print of a horse's hoof is in a stone.
38495: A witch enters the house through the keyhole.
38496: A sick child is given asafoetida in his drink and a little bag of asafoetida on his chest. The next day he is cured. Two wreaths are found in his pillow and thrown into the stove, after which the cats go wild. One cat gets a kick, and the next day a man is limping; he must be the one who bewitched the boy.
38501: A man who sees funerals and all their details beforehand has to get up at night. Later he has to attend the funerals.
38505: Never walk in the middle of the street at night, because then you can be pushed aside when a phantom funeral procession passes.
38506: A dog howling eerily means a death.
38507: Omens of a death are black crows in the farmyard, chattering magpies near the house, the ringing of a bell at a funeral, and burial on a Monday.
38508: Children hear singing at a place where the Salvation Army later holds meetings.
38511: A woman no longer dares to go home alone because she was suddenly flung off the road.
38512: Before the train ran, people heard the sound of a train.
38513: A woman predicts carts driving without horses and carts flying through the air, that is, the car and the aeroplane.
38516: Near a haunted house two men twice see a man standing in the middle of the fields. The third time, however, he has vanished.
38517: A black dog as big as a calf walks with a young man for a while on a pitch-dark evening, and suddenly vanishes.
38520: Two girls whose throats were cut haunt the area.
38521: The sound of a man being run over and killed by a train was heard beforehand.
38522: The sound of a man who had lain down in front of the train being run over was heard beforehand.
38525: If the palls are too long, the dead come back.
38526: A man does not keep his promise to his late wife that his second wife will not wear her clothes. At first the man ignores his daughter's message that her mother has come back and knocks on the window and door during the day. He meets his first wife anyway; when he asks what she wants, she answers that she wants her clothes. When the second wife asks who has her clothes, the dead woman grabs her by the sleeve and cries that she is wearing her clothes.
38528: Sons of a witch cannot do magic, and therefore cannot fly on a broomstick either.
38534: A man can fix people to the spot and make them do what he says, such as drinking milk from a saucer or crowing like a rooster; he makes women's skirts fall down, and when he is imprisoned he can get doors open.
38535: The devil's footprint is in a stone at the spot where he jumped over a canal.
38546: A man hears singing in the churchyard at night, but nothing can be seen.
38547: After the farmer and his wife were murdered in the cowshed of a farm, a lot of noise comes from the shed. The farm has been demolished.
38548: A man sees a house on fire before it really burns down. Many do not believe it, but it comes true.
38550: A fisherman complains that he always catches devilishly small eels. After he catches a fat eel with glowing eyes, he never fishes again, because the eel was the devil.
38551: A man plays at being a minister and mocks everything in his sermon. He never does it again, because at night the devil came to his bed.
38563: A ghostly gentleman and lady walk straight through gates.
38564: The people who were digging for a chest of money stopped because blood ran down their bodies.
38565: On his deathbed a man sees three hearses. He dies, and so do the two neighbours next to him.
38567: A woman sees that not Veenwouden but Hoek will become the village.
38568: A woman predicts that the cemetery will be located in a certain place.
38570: Do not walk in the middle of the road at night, because then you can be pushed aside.
38571: A dog howling eerily and a group of magpies mean a death.
38572: The neighbours turn out to know what was talked about during a visit. Every evening a strange cat sits on the windowsill. One evening a black cat that brushes against a man's legs gets a kick. The next day the neighbour woman turns out to be wounded on her head.
38574: A foal with a porridge pot around its neck walks about at night.
38575: Hearing hammering at a shipyard at night means work is coming again.
38576: A man can take away toothache. He is also afraid of nothing, not even of a being hovering above the water that comes towards him.
38578: At night a man sees someone walking behind a cart, praying. His companions see nothing.
38582: A man walking around the farmyard at night sees a being come flying towards him. It is the punishment for walking around the farmyard.
38584: Some people saw the lights of the tram before the tram began to run.
38585: Invoking the devil, a young man says that no one can jump as far as he can. Then someone jumps over the canal. Since then there has been a human foot on one side and a horse's hoof on the other in a stone slab, for it was the devil.
38591: A man with a wisseldaalder (ever-returning coin) often comes back from shopping with more money. The wisseldaalder keeps coming back, but must never be spent entirely, or it disappears. Whoever has a wisseldaalder is sold to the devil.
38595: Witches cannot be hit with a bullet, but they can be hit with a silver dime.
38596: Unknown haunting at a certain place.
38598: A fortune teller predicts that of three young men one will have children, another will stay a bachelor and the third is on the black card. It comes true; the third man dies not long afterwards.
38605: A person cannot say just anything. A woman who says she does not want children never gets that far, for she is run over and killed by the tram.
38607: The money a man received from a woman has, when he looks at it closely, turned into oak leaves.
38609: Woman sticks pins into the chests of dolls representing her victims.
38612: The print of the hoof of the devil, who jumped over a canal from east to west, can still be seen.
38613: Some people see ghosts, such as a man who sees something one evening and becomes terribly frightened.
38616: A dog howling eerily means a death in the area. A clock ticking fast also means a death.
38617: Magpies and rooks near the house mean a death. The rook is the gravedigger or bearer, the magpie is the messenger.
38618: After the devil has got hold of a man who says he is not afraid of the devil, this man never again says he is not afraid of the devil.
38619: A policeman who has to see to the closing of the cafés gets tipsy from the drinks every landlord gives him. He then curses and mocks freely. He does so too when one time he cannot light his pipe because of the strong wind. But he refuses the live coal offered to him by a beautiful woman who suddenly stands before him. It would have been his death, for it was the devil.
38623: People hear hammering in the evening although no hammering was actually going on. Later a house was built on that spot.
38624: People see a house on fire, although in reality it is not. The house later burns down.
38625: The wilde lantaarn (wild lantern, will-o'-the-wisp) is a portent of bicycle lamps.
38626: The place where a girl drowned is haunted.
38629: After midnight do not walk in the middle of the road, because if a phantom funeral procession passes you can be pushed away.
38630: In the dark one evening a boy encounters something large that has disappeared again a little later.
38631: In the dark a little man comes walking beside a girl.
38632: Something hovering is uncanny, so a man runs away fast.
38633: A large black dog walks with a married couple at night. The woman sees the dog, but her husband does not. After the woman says that a dog is walking beside them, the dog gradually disappears.
38634: A drunk man who has used coarse language in the pub is flung away by the devil.
38635: People hear organ playing and singing at the place where a church is later built.
38636: A minister tells that people hear a voice from the water saying that the time has come, but the man has not. Shortly afterwards a carriage drives into the canal, and the man in the carriage drowns.
38639: Children are frightened with a foal that haunts the area with a porridge pot around its neck.
38641: Children are afraid of a place where a girl in white walks in the evening.
38642: The barn doors of a house fly open by themselves.
38643: The doors of haunted barns open by themselves at night. Churning mills also start turning there at night, and there are places where no one can sleep, because one is lifted up and thrown away.
38646: A witch can change herself into a black cat. The cats sometimes meet in a meadow, where they meow.
38657: A dog howling eerily means a death in the area.
38659: Whoever looks into a black mirror can discover whom they will marry.
38661: When the dogs begin to howl eerily, a death will soon follow.
38662: Someone is born with a caul and can see funeral processions passing. You must not walk in the middle of the road, otherwise you will be flung aside by the funeral procession.
38667: Little lights are a voorloop (an apparition foreshadowing an event) of the tram.
38668: Some people see a funeral procession at night; it is a portent of a death.
38669: You should not walk in the middle of the road, because of a funeral procession that may pass by.
38672: A girl is ill through bewitchment. A witch's wreath is found in her pillow and burnt. People wait for the witch with a gun. A magpie sounds at the chimney and is shot at. The bird is not hit, but the girl recovers.
38674: Witte wieven (white women) can also haunt.
38675: The eerie howling of a dog announces a death.
38682: A witch in the form of a hare has an eye shot out. The woman herself claimed that she lost her eye because of an illness.
38683: Witches can turn themselves into cats. Someone was once given two apples by a witch, but over time they turned into toads.
38688: In de Pein a black dog runs around. People claim it is a plaagbeest (tormenting beast).
38689: Old Sweitse Oldenburger lived by a pond. Every night at 12 o'clock he saw his dead wife running around the pond. She came to sit with him and could find no rest. That was his punishment for always having treated her so badly.
38690: Sweitse Oldenburger tells that he was once out in the boat when he came upon something by a gate. It was the devil with a wide-open mouth, roaring loudly. From then on he was converted and never did anything wicked again.
38691: Some people send out an empty bottle with a jack of spades card in it. A little later a full bottle of gin arrives in its place. But the one who sent out the card may not touch the full bottle.
38693: Old Albert Gjaltema had a wisseldaalder (ever-returning coin). Because of it he always had money, for it never ran out.
38698: Janne treated her husband badly, but she did not dare to be alone after he died, and he comes at night in a long black coat and hat to the attic, where things got wild.
38699: After his death, Durkje's husband sits in front of the house at night.
39369: All kinds of superstitions are listed.
39579: Hares and black dogs are animals of ill omen. Dogs with brown spots above their eyes are "spokenkijkers" (ghost-seers); they can see spirits.
41161: A farmer who treats his stepson badly sees his own funeral from the attic window.
41169: Because of an agreement, the devil must move sand in barrels. But the barrels have no bottoms, and so sand hills came into being (De Duvelsbulten of Wedde).
41170: Not only death, but also the building of a factory, railway, canal or house can be preceded by an omen.
42515:
According to many people, a black cat coming from the left brings bad luck.
In the past, an entrail reader could make predictions from the position of the entrails of dead animals and people.
Bird augurs studied birds in the sky. On that basis they made predictions.
42521: About: names for the devil, devilish animals and devilish card playing.
42544: About Friday the thirteenth, horseshoes and knocking on wood.
42553: The narrator knows from hearsay that people used to say that spirits of the dead dwelt in peat bogs and fen areas.
42594: The interviewee says that during a working holiday in Norway he stayed on a farm haunted by a ghost. It was a great-grandmother of the farming couple who lived there. Because of this, noises were often heard and the lights went out. The narrator experienced it himself once.
42595: Witte wieven (white women) can lead you astray: they make you lose your way.
42599: The copper scroll from Qumran contains clues to an enormous treasure, which the Jews are said to have brought out of Egypt. No one has yet found the enormous treasure of gold.
42604: Seeing a black cat and walking under a ladder bring bad luck.
42605: Witches do the same as believers: witches call on a power to get something done. They call on the Power of Nature instead of God. I don't find today's witches special anymore: nowadays they can't do anything, like fly on a broom. Witches used to be able to do much more.
42611: To find out whether she was a witch, a woman was thrown into the water. If she floated, she was a witch and was thrown on the pyre. If she sank, she was dead all the same.
42615: The Romans believed that three crows flying side by side brought bad luck.
42616: The devil appears in the shape of goats and billy goats.
42620: Witches occupy themselves with natural forces and natural remedies. In the past they threw them on the pyre.
42630: To identify a witch, people had a small baby poo. Then they burnt the excrement in the hearth. Whoever came in then was the witch: she would be drawn by the smell of the burnt excrement.
42853: The interviewee talks about omens and about lucky and unlucky days. Black ravens are associated with misfortune and death. She does not believe in Friday the thirteenth herself, though she would not want to marry on that day. She does know someone who got married on the thirteenth on purpose. Wednesday used to be a lucky day, because suitors were allowed to meet each other on that day.
42861: People do believe in wilde wieven (wild women), but white ones? Not apart from the wedding.
42871: Will-o'-the-wisps are spirits of dead people who lure others into the marsh. These stories occur mainly around peat bogs and arise from the fact that gas in these bogs can ignite spontaneously and is seen as a will-o'-the-wisp.
42873:
A member of a witches' circle says that she used to hear many stories about witte wieven (white women). She had an experience with them herself as a teenager, when a wisp of cold fog slid along her throat. Still, she plays it down by saying she would not have taken it for a witte wief if she had not known the stories.
Her witches' circle has recently started calling itself 'de witte wieven'. In the witches' café people can come to them with questions about Wicca.
42875:
Apparitions are regarded as negative in the interviewee's area. On the hill called the 'zwarte dam' (black dam) nothing will grow any more since a monk once died there.
The rich farmer Geert Loche was so miserly that all his life he declared he would always guard his land well against riffraff. After his death he walked a silent round along his land, but had to stop when some people pitched their camp on his path. The rest of the time he had to haunt the place in a rage.
42877:
Black cats and hellhounds are associated with misfortune. Black crows are harbingers of death.
When a spider makes a tear in its web, it means a storm is coming. For if a spider makes a tear itself, it can repair its web more easily after the storm.
42886:
According to the interviewee, witches have nothing to do with the devil. The devil is associated with cats, swans and crows.
Witches are always associated with cats. The interviewee does not know a single Wiccan who has no cat.
The interviewee knew no stories about ghost animals. She did say she had the feeling that her own dead cat still haunted the house.
42895: In the old burial mound 'Hersenberg' witte wieven (white women) used to be spotted. Now a sweet little witch called 'harsje' lives there. She is said to be a pitiful case. The interviewee knows no old source for this story.
42899: The interviewee talks about omens of death, burial customs and how she buried her own pets.
42913: To keep the nightmare out, one must place the slippers upside down in front of the bed, otherwise the horse would come inside.
43167: Saying that there is a witch in the churn when the butter will not come. Pouring hot water into the churn, sometimes while reciting a rhyme, to get the witch out of the churn.
43169: Belief in omens of death, such as a dog howling behind the house, or a magpie or crow flying against the window.
43170: A man sees events that happen later.
43540: A broken mirror means bad luck or death.
43544: Black ravens are never good. When a dove or another bird flies into the room, it means misfortune. When a bird taps on the window, it means good news.
43551: The Damavoi [phonetic spelling] is the good guardian spirit of the house. He is depicted with a long white beard. There are spirits in the rivers, and in trees too. The spirit of the tree, the evil one, is green. A house can also have a poltergeist.
43560:
A Russian woman has her future foretold by a spirit. The letters 'JOH' appear, but these letters do not occur in that combination in the Russian alphabet. Later she marries a Dutchman named Johan.
The woman often has premonitions, for example about an accident, or about the moment she should phone her mother in Russia.
43591: A card reader's prediction that a girl will marry a fisherman, that he will drown and that she will have many children comes true.
43595: A bicycle is seen with no one riding it. People are also afraid of white figures.
43636: A swearing man is struck off the road and cannot be found. The devil must have taken him.
43637: The black horses that walk along the dike and suddenly vanish are devils.
43638: One evening a couple sees two men with a lantern between them. They avoid the apparition three times; the last time the apparition bursts apart. Their aunt does not want to believe it, but through a gap in the shutters she sees the ghost, which then bursts apart.
43641: At night the churn is heard without a horse walking, but nothing can be seen.
43643: Stopping a wizard by making a cross over the planks across a ditch.
43644: A scoffer is frightened by a phantom funeral procession he meets one evening.
43992: During the war with the Indies there were clairvoyants going around in Groningen who could tell whether soldiers were still alive or had been killed.
43994: At the Galgenlaantje in Uiterburen it was sometimes haunted.
44787: Possibility that a dead man comes back.
44788: Stories from the past about a ghost dog.
45492: Psychics sense events in the vicinity of the churchyard and the convent.
45736: The Walfriduskerk is built on cow hides.
46284: Belief in ghosts and witches; women are quickly called sorcerers.
46286: In case of illness, someone goes to a devil banisher, who gives a little bottle of liquid. He warns not to say anything to anyone on the way and to keep the bottle safe in a pocket. Someone, the devil, tries to crush the bottle.
46288: Experiences of night-mares. The night-mare is one of the seven daughters in a family. The night-mare squeezes the throat shut; it disappears with prayer.
46504: On Ameland, fishermen saw ghostly horses at night between Hollum and Ballum.
47026: Coming home one evening, a man sees a coffin with a corpse, from which he cuts a piece of hair. The next morning he sees in the mirror that he himself is missing a piece of hair. He leaves the farm, but on a visit the following winter he falls ill and dies.
47028: When a man comes home drunk at night, everything starts moving; in the morning all is quiet.
47036: Old people never walk in the middle of the road, but always at the side, to avoid walking into a funeral procession.
47040: A woman born with a caul sees funerals in advance and who will walk in the funeral procession.
48502: A fisherman sees a ghostly apparition in Urk clothing and with long hair. He thinks it might well be his mother, whom he never knew.
48903: If you throw an apple peel in one piece on the ground, you get the name of the man or woman you will marry.
50504: On a farm the doors open by themselves. A butcher's hand who says he is not afraid wants to witness it, but believes it is haunting. The owner also experiences the haunting and sets the farm on fire. When it is further demolished, corpses turn out to be buried under the stable.
50512: A farmer has a pact with the devil, because the gates of the drive open by themselves.
50513: On a mill yard a witte juffer (white lady) haunts in the evening.
50515: It is haunted on a small island where a churchyard used to be. The ships that anchored there in the evening are found adrift the next morning.
50516: When a man dies, the treasure he found is still undivided. The two youngest sons keep the treasure for themselves by saying the devil is coming to fetch their father, since he sold his soul. The two eldest disappear out of fear.
50521: Haunting in a churchyard begins after the death of the mother of three sisters who live behind the churchyard.
50523: On a farm, knocking and strange noises are heard, especially in the front room. The noises stop as soon as it gets light.
50524: A minister believes that something once happened on a farm that was not right.
50525: A yellowish light or glow is seen on a farm. A mother-in-law says their maid dries clothes by the fire, and neighbours see a yellow light at night.
50526: From outside a house seems to be on fire because of a yellowish light in the living room; inside everything is dark.
50527: Someone says he has to go to a farm because there is a strange light.
50528: A man often sees a light on a farm, but thinks it is none of his business.
50529: A coloured, glittering bank of mist hangs above the roof of a stable.
50539: At the place where a monastery once stood, a headless man may appear on a dusky evening.
50540: A church is built on ox hides and stands on the spot chosen by oxen.
50542: In the evening a man sees flames by the roof of a farm.
50543: A woman borrows money from her neighbour and forgets to pay it back. After her death, the neighbour one evening stands on the rain barrel with her hand outstretched. When the borrowed sum is put out in the evening, it is gone the next morning, and the loan is repaid.
50544: Father goes to a duivelbanner (exorcist) for his bewitched child, who gives him a potion and herbs, advising him to pay close attention on the way. On the way the bottle breaks when he is pushed by a woman he recognises as a friend of his wife. At midnight the cradle and room are fumigated with the herbs, while the door is rattled and cats go wild. When the man looks down through a crack in the floor, he sees his wife's friend standing by the cradle with a little doll into which she sticks needles. The man speaks to her, after which the woman trips over the fire pot and dies of her burns.
51040: A farmer is troubled by ghosts in his stable. Farmhands dare not live with him because they are afraid of the four figures that come down from the loft at night with a table, chairs and a candle. The farmer offers a reward to whoever can rid him of the ghosts. Hans dares to try. He spends the night in the stable and sees the figures take money from a hiding place and count it. When they see it is all still there, they pray to God, asking when they will have done enough penance. Hans and the farmer take the money from the hiding place and share it. The next night the four figures come down from the loft again. When they see the money is gone, they thank God. The haunting has stopped for good.
57813: In Stiens lived a farmer who had sold his soul to the devil. When the devil comes to fetch him, he asks whether he may button up his doublet. The devil gives permission. The man says he will never button up his doublet again and is therefore free. The devil is furious and flies out of the window, against the wall of the neighbouring house. He hits it so hard that the print of his horse's hoof is left behind, which remained visible for forty years.
57815: A farmer and his family play cards late into the evening in wintertime. This is wrong for two reasons: a farming family must go to bed at nine, because they have to get up early the next morning, and card playing is an invention of the devil. One evening a stranger asks for a place to sleep, and when he sees them playing cards, he asks if he may join. He wins every time. When one of those present looks under the table to pick up a card, he sees that the stranger has a horse's hoof: it is the devil. The devil hands out a beating and shouts as he flies away: 'Nine o'clock, bed!' Since then no one plays cards anymore, and at nine o'clock they hear a voice urging the family to go to bed. Once, when there are guests, the company does not go to bed at nine. The stranger comes again and hands out a sound beating. When later a farmer who reads the Bible a great deal in the evenings lives in the same house, the calling at nine o'clock is no longer heard.
57901: In a Frisian village there are many witches. To recognise the witches, the village boys came up with something: they cross the path of passing women with their clog. If the women are innocent, this will not bother them; if they are witches, they will be forced to stop because of the cross shape. The witches devised a countermeasure and made sure that all women stopped whenever this happened. The boys' habit was soon forbidden by the village constable.
57902: A man gets a pancake from his neighbour. Because he suspects her of witchcraft, he does not eat it but puts the pancake away. After a few days the pancake turns out to have changed into a toad. The toad is burned. While this happens, the witch walks around the house wailing.
57903: A boy sees a large cat prowling around his parents' house. He does not trust it and hits the cat on the head with a stick. The next day the neighbour woman turns out to have a wound on her head: she was the cat.
57904: In Stroobos it once happened that people set a rat trap in the attic and found a black cat in it. The cat is caught by its right front paw and is freed. The next day the cleaning woman lets them know that she hurt her right arm during the night and cannot come to work...
57905: A man sees his wife's clothes lying on the floor. When a big cat comes along and wants to crawl into them, he kicks the cat, but... it turns out to be his wife.
57906: A group of boys chases a large black cat, which they suspect of being a witch, with stones and clubs. The cat is wounded on a hind leg. The next day an old woman who was suspected of being a witch turns out to be lame.
57907: Women who went out peddling with baskets on a yoke were often taken for witches. In the evening they were said to ride home on the yoke. In Garijp there lived a woman who peddled bread rolls and was said to be able to fly with her baskets of wares on her arms. A hunter once shot at a strange-looking bird. The bird was hit and a basket of rolls came falling down. The bird itself, however, was not seen. Still, this was taken as proof that the roll seller was a witch.
57911: Witches can fly by rubbing themselves with magic ointment and speaking a spell. When a farmer discovers that his wife is a witch, she asks him whether he wants to take a trip with her. She teaches him a magic formula. The man makes a mistake in saying it and flies not over things but through them, which is painful.
57912: Witches can change into more than just cats. In Molkwerum witches changed into hares that milked the cows, so that the farmer had no milk left.
57918: A farmer and his wife have a little son, Fokke. Every day, not long after the farmhand Abe goes to work, the child becomes restless and cries for hours. The farmer and his wife fear witchcraft and do not trust Abe. Abe, however, swears he has nothing to do with it. When Abe comes home, his wife has the kettle on the fire, she says to boil potatoes for the pig. But she already did that the day before, and Abe grows suspicious. The next day he spies on his wife while she thinks he is at work. Again she puts the kettle on the fire and takes out two dolls. She calls the first doll Griet, the daughter of the peat skipper who sold her bad peat. She presses the doll's little feet against the hot kettle to torment the girl. She calls the second doll Fokke, the farmer's son. He too must be tormented, because the farmer's wife sells her butter too dearly. Abe storms in and says it must stop. His wife begs him not to tell anyone. Abe goes to the farmer, where it turns out Fokke is much better.
57920: A man and a woman have a child who is always ill. They fear witchcraft. The man goes to a duivelbanner (exorcist) for advice. He gives him a potion they must give the child daily and herbs they must burn to cleanse the cradle. He warns the man that the witch will try to prevent the child from recovering. He must therefore watch whom he meets on the way. He must also make sure all doors and windows are firmly shut while the herbs are burned. When the man is nearly home, a woman comes toward him and bumps into him. This breaks the bottle of medicine. His wife tells him that a friend of hers, who always shows great interest in the sick child, had just left. While the duivelbanner's herbs are burning, the door is rattled, and a little later they hear terrible caterwauling. The next day the whole town knows what has happened, and the friend is suspected of being a witch. Her husband spies on her and discovers that she has a little doll into which she sticks needles. The man takes the doll from her and burns it. The woman moans with pain, and when the doll has burned completely, the woman is dead.
57921: The youngest child of a skipper and his wife is sickly. The parents suspect witchcraft is involved, and the mother decides to go to a devil-banisher for advice. He advises her to keep the child's urine and to buy a small earthenware pan and a packet of pins. She must put the pins and the urine in the pan and bring it to the boil. When she does this, the witch may come to the house and walk around it wailing, or, if she is far away, the witch will suffer great pain in her own house. The mother does as told, but no one comes to the house. From then on the child gets better. Some time later the woman goes with her child to her former home town. There she meets the little daughter of the old midwife who used to help her with her children. The girl tells her that her mother had been in great pain one day some time ago. The woman understands that this old midwife must have been the witch who bewitched her child.
57922: The two youngest children of a couple are sickly. The father decides to go to a devil-banisher. He tells him to examine the children's pillows and give them medicine. None of it helps. One day a woman comes to the door who knows there is illness in the house. The livestock is not healthy either. The woman has the father drill holes in beams in the stable. She puts powder in the holes, and then the holes can be closed again with pegs. The woman says that the one doing them harm is someone they know, who was also present at the birth of some of their children. The parents suspect their old midwife. The woman warns the couple that the next day someone will come asking for something white, which they must not give. The next day the midwife comes asking for milk, but she is not given it. The helpful woman returns and gives the parents a small bag of herbs, which must be burnt. While the herbs are burning, the midwife walks around the house wailing. After this the children recover.
57925: To identify witches, oil with needles or pins in it can be boiled; the witch is then tormented. Someone with a special coin can also see who the witch is: she then wears a small frying pan on her head. While the oil is boiling, a witch may have an accident at home; the witch is then marked for life.
57936: The churning can be bewitched: the milk then foams out of the churn and the butter does not separate. To counter this, a little bag of herbs from the duivelbanner (exorcist) can be hung in the churn. To prevent it, it is wise to bury a little bag of asafoetida in the cowshed, or better still, under the threshold of the house.
57939:
Farmers planted lovage in front of the milk cellar to ward off witches.
On poor soil people sometimes found a substance that looked like butter but did not have the same properties. This was the work of witches.
Usually old women are accused of witchcraft. It is said of them that in the evening they hang their purse on the front door to receive money from the devil, but they are usually poor all the same.
An old woman once pretended she could do witchcraft to command respect.
57946: The devil plays a large role in folk belief. Whoever makes a pact with the devil can perform supernatural feats. Sorcerers and witches are Satan's accomplices. In Friesland bewitching is called 'tsjoenen' (doing harm) and a witch is called a 'tsjoenster' (evildoer). Devil-banishers also have special powers, but they use them against evil. In particular they thwart witches in their attempts to kill a person or an animal (according to the pact with the devil, a witch must bewitch someone to death every seven years; if she fails, the witch herself must die).
57948:
To learn witchcraft one must renounce God and pledge loyalty to the devil. Out of hypocrisy witches do come to church, but they sit there with their backs to the minister.
All witches can turn themselves into cats. In Wommels a fine black cat with white paws was seen for a while. When one day an old woman died and her body was laid out, it was discovered that under her overskirt she wore a black skirt with four white patches sewn onto it. The black cat with white paws was never seen again...
57950: It is dangerous to accept an apple or other fruit from an unknown woman. If you do, you must cut a piece off before you eat from it. If the giver is a witch, eating from it straight away can give you a toad in your stomach. You must never answer three questions in a row from a witch with 'yes', or you will fall into her power. Lending fire or salt to a witch is also very dangerous, so lend these only to people you trust.
60727: There were people who could send the jack of clubs playing card for gin. The one who sends the jack of clubs may not himself accept the bottle offered at the door. Often no one in the company dares to do this, but if someone does, the following happens: the devil's conjurer throws the jack of clubs outside and tells it to fetch a bottle of gin. A little later the one who will accept the bottle must stick his arm outside: on the bottle offered to him lies the jack of clubs. The first glass is thrown over the shoulder and is for the bringer. Not everyone dared to drink gin obtained this way, because this drink was said to come from the devil.
60729: People of whom it was unclear how they came by their money were often thought to have made a pact with the devil and to receive money from him. They were also often suspected of being Freemasons. It is said of Freemasons that their meetings are chaired by the devil and that children are eaten at their gatherings.
60731:
With a wisseldaalder (ever-returning coin) you were never short of money. Every time you bought something for less than a daalder, you got change and the daalder returned to your pocket by itself. You did have to be careful not to spend the daalder all at once, or you lost it for good.
You could get a wisseldaalder by going to a crossroads with a cat in a sack and calling there: "Who will buy my little hare?". The devil would then appear and ask what animal was in the sack; you must not answer that it was a cat, but say it was a hare, which would cost a daalder. The devil bought the cat in the sack in exchange for a wisseldaalder and a promise of loyalty to the devil. The devil let the cat go again, but it was no longer an ordinary cat, but a witch.
If you no longer wanted the wisseldaalder, you could pass it on to someone else, provided the other person made the same vow of loyalty.
60748: At the end of the nineteenth century a card reader lived in Leeuwarden, Akke van 't Vliet, also called Akke Kaart. Many people used Akke's services, including the well-to-do. But it was mainly servant girls who asked her for advice. It is said of Akke Kaart's death that she was found with her neck wrung. This was done by the devil, in whose service she was.
60757: In Friesland it was said that there was a 'black mirror' in Amsterdam. In this mirror you could get to see your future beloved. Behind a wall of glass you saw a beautiful garden in which your beloved would appear with the number of children you would have together. If there was no love in store for you, you saw a mourning room with a coffin in it. This did not mean you would die soon, but that you would remain alone. The beloved shown was the soul of the person you would later marry. The soul of the boy or girl temporarily left the body to show itself in the black mirror. The beloved's body then briefly fainted. When the boy or girl came to, he or she remembered having dreamed about his or her beloved. Later, stalls appeared at fairs in Friesland called 'Mirror of Love' or 'Mirror of Secrets'. These were popularly called the 'black mirror'.
69236: A girl wished to see her sweetheart, a sailor who had been away on a voyage for a long time. A friend told her that there was a sorceress in Leeuwarden who could make this possible. This woman filled a tub with water and told the girl to look into it. The girl saw her sweetheart sitting on board a ship eating an apple. Now she knew for certain that he was healthy. When the sweetheart returned to his beloved after his voyage, he told her that one day, while eating an apple, he had suddenly had a fainting fit out of nowhere. The girl told him what she had seen at the sorceress's, and they understood that he had fainted at the moment his soul travelled to Leeuwarden.
69240:
In Bolsward lived a man addicted to drink and card playing. He often promised his wife he would mend his ways, but kept falling back into his old habits. Once he cried out: "May the devil tear me limb from limb if I get drunk again!" After this things went well for a while, but one evening he came home drunk from the tavern again. He lay down to sleep on the hearthstone. In the morning his wife found nothing but a little heap of ashes in front of the hearth and a black handprint on the white wall. This print had to come from the devil: although it was whitewashed over, the print remained visible. To many this proved that the devil had burned the man.
Dykstra regards this story as a misreading of the story of Douwe Sydses, who fell asleep drunk in front of the hearth, which was no longer burning, and in the night went up in flames. People did believe this must be the work of the devil, but according to Balthasar Bekker, who recorded the story, this is nonsense. It is not inexplicable that a man as drunk as Douwe Sydses should catch fire.
69241: In Makkum lived a skipper who made such short voyages that he was suspected of having made a pact with the devil. When the skipper was on the return voyage from Riga to Makkum, the crew noticed something strange: the captain seemed to be in lively conversation with someone, yet in the middle of the sea no one could have come aboard. A boy is sent to look into the cabin. Frightened, he says he saw the skipper talking with a man dressed in red. When the others come to see for themselves, the cabin is empty. A porthole is open, though. The mate suspects the man in red was the devil and that he flew off with the skipper through the porthole. Afterwards no one dared sail on the ship again.
69242:
A young man lost his wife and wished that she could come back to him. After her funeral his wife suddenly came back to him. She looked just as she used to. They lived happily together for a long time and had children. When one day the woman was shown a cross, she turned out to be the devil, who had appeared to the man in her shape as punishment for his foolish wish.
A similar story tells how the wife of a farmer who was always cursing ran away from home one day. She was not found anywhere, but her shoes were discovered by the lock. After a week the woman suddenly came back. She asked her husband not to curse any more and promised to stay with him. The couple had nine daughters. When one day the farmer flew into a rage and cursed, the woman disappeared into the cellar. The man found her clothes there in a heap. The woman had been the devil. The farmer's real wife had drowned herself; her body had been washed out to sea. The daughters all turned out to be witches, as were their children and grandchildren.
69243: Sometimes the devil frightens sinners so badly that they repent and from then on walk the right path. In this way the devil actually works against himself.
69244: At the fair in Baard, young people kept dancing during a violent storm. Some joked that they could dance by the light of the lightning. The devil appeared and danced on the windowsill on one leg.
69245: A boy wants to be initiated into the art of sorcery. For this he visits a devil-conjurer. But he is so shocked by the oath he must swear that he renounces the devil. The devil-conjurer vanishes at once.
69246: A boy in Spannum wanted to make the villagers believe that he had been leapt upon by a strange creature late one evening. The animal jumped onto his back and threw its claws over the boy's shoulders. The boy tried to run away, but the creature would not let go. Only when he called on God did the creature leave him. In the days that followed he pretended to be converted, but in reality he turned out to still be a sinner.
69326: A ghostly foal haunted the area near Heerenveen. A drunkard who still had a long walk home from Heerenveen once boasted that if he met the foal, he would jump on its back, use his garter as a bridle and ride it home. When he actually met the animal, he tried to walk around it, but the horse kept blocking his way. In the end he did jump on its back. The drunkard got home that night, but how, he does not really know.
69329: A glowing foal haunted the Leppedijk. A farm girl had stayed in the village until late and had to go home alone. When she was warned about the ghost foal, she claimed she would put her garter in its mouth and ride it home. But when she actually met the animal, she was terrified and ran home.
69333: In some places flayed horses or kedden (small horses) haunted the area. A foal haunted the road between Hijum and Hallum. It always walked part of the way with the people it met and then vanished again. A farmhand met the ghost animal. Again the foal walked along with him, but when they reached the farm it did not vanish, but kept blocking the door. After the farmhand cried out in anger, "That devilish thing!", he received a blow that knocked him down. When he got up again, the animal was gone. It has never been seen since.
69336: People used to tell of a devilish creature called a 'plaagbeest' (plague beast) or 'pestdier' (pest animal). Such an animal was black, had four legs and eyes as big as saucers that glowed in the dark. It was seen as the bringer of plague and other diseases. A farmer once met a plague beast at night; his horses refused to go any further.
69346: On Schiermonnikoog a skipper once found a rooster. It let itself be caught easily and the skipper put it in a sack. On the way the man noticed that the sack was getting heavier and heavier. In the end he could no longer hold it and dropped the sack. The rooster suddenly vanished. Only blue, stinking smoke remained. The skipper realised he had been dealing with the devil.
69348: A father and son were once badly frightened by what they thought was a plaagbeest (plague beast). It turned out, however, to be a shoemaker who had thrown a calfskin over his head.
69757: A skater manages to skate even faster than the devil.
69771:
Discussion of ghostly phenomena: the dead who return because something was left unfinished. Certain Reformed Protestants find this inconsistent with their faith. Whoever meets a ghost must say a formula:
If you are from God, speak; if you are from the devil, go away.
69772: A ghost dog was said to roam the Eewal in Leeuwarden. The Zuipsteeg in particular was said to be very unsafe. Passers-by were pushed towards the water by an invisible force. When gaslight came to the town, the apparition went away, and the water has been filled in with earth.
69774: Someone living outside Leeuwarden, who had been to the city on business, came back late in the evening. He walked calmly past the Olde Galileën, but a little further on he saw that the land beside the lime works was completely covered with cats, which soon disappeared, however. But things did not get better: for all the trestles at the lime works actually began to dance like anything. The man naturally took to his heels.
69775: On the Vliet in Leeuwarden there stood a windmill on which people never dared to put red sails, because they were sure it would then catch fire.
69776: The cap of a dead skipper keeps haunting the place where he died. A man who would not believe the story went to look and got the cap on his head. The cap could no longer be taken off his head and from then on he had to walk around with it. Since then the cap no longer haunts.
69777: The following happened to a young man from Sexbierum: one Saturday-to-Sunday night, coming back from courting, he met a man without a head on the road near Lankum, a small country estate near Franeker. The suitor had to cross a dam, and there the apparition brushed past him. The suitor took to his heels and so could give no further account of what the headless man was doing.
69778: Skipper Uilke Annes of Hindeloopen goes goose hunting on Christmas Eve. But he cannot hit a single bird and becomes very angry. At one point he thinks he has finally found a flock of geese to shoot at. He even thinks he sees a swan among them! But the swan turns out to be an apparition that keeps growing and scares the wits out of the man. In the end he manages to get home safely.
69779: A deceased minister keeps haunting the churchyard. Three friends walk home across the churchyard. Two of them boast that they could handle the minister's ghost if it appeared now. The ghost then takes the two boasters away. The third gets off with a fright. Four weeks later the two friends who were taken turn up again, but they do not tell what happened.
69780: A hill near Rijs in Gaasterland is called the Spookberg (Ghost Hill). Not many years ago, a suitor coming back from his sweetheart at night took the path through the wood over this hill, as the shortest way home. But when he reached the Spookberg, he saw a figure approaching from the wood, most like a calf, greyish in colour. A short distance ahead of the young man the ghost dashed across the road. No sooner had it disappeared into the trees again than the suitor fled, fearing the ghost animal would follow him.
69781: Near Bakhuizen it happened only a few years ago that two men were busy loading a wagon of hay in the field on a Saturday evening. This was the last of the hay harvest they had to bring in, so they were keen to get it done. But although it was at the time of the longest summer days, it had already grown dark; a thick mist was also rising over the field, so that the two men could no longer see each other. Just one small pile of hay still had to go on the wagon and then it would be done. The one standing on the ground to pass it up to his mate called: Take it! but received no answer. He called again, but in vain. On looking, he found that his mate had disappeared, and so he too set off home. When he got there he learned that Sunday had begun. The last hay had to stay in the field until Monday morning.
69782: The schoolmaster of Koudum mocks a ghostly event. That very evening, while winding the tower clock, he believes he is visited by the devil. Several villagers claim to have seen and heard the apparition of the devil after it came running out of the bell tower. Some know-it-alls, however, claim the apparition was really a goat that had broken loose.
69784: A butcher walks home in the dark. On reaching the Hoogezand, he thinks he sees two witches. Not long after, he sees a silent figure that seems to come up onto the dike. The man fears it is the devil and runs off. Twice more he meets the figure. Each time he calls out a greeting, but the figure does not answer. The third time the butcher strikes the figure with his stick, but it makes no sound. The man is so frightened by this that he starts screaming. When he reaches the village, people think he has been beaten up by the devil. The man himself claims it was he who beat the devil. His stick was found broken in two by a stone post on the dike, where several posts stand at equal distances from each other.
69785: In Oudemirdum a man without a head was still haunting as late as September 1890.
69786: At a farmhouse at Baansterburen near Rauwerd a ghost used to be seen as well. At night an old woman stood there by the turnstile gate through which one came on and off the farmyard. This gate could never be kept shut at night, whatever one did. Even if it was carefully closed in the evening, in the morning it was always open.
69787: It is still uncanny on the Hooidammen, between Sint Nicolaasga and Doniaga. One evening Johannes Reinders came back late from the fields, and the field gate he had to go through opened by itself and, once he was through, closed again by itself. When he reached the Hooidammen, he suddenly felt a heavy, crushing weight on one of his shoulders. A little later it jumped over to the other shoulder, and when the man had passed the dams, he felt free again.
69788: Years ago a white lady walked at night in Legemeer. A few reckless young men who went out one Sunday evening to pay the lady a visit, as they mockingly put it, came off badly. - Many a ghost story ends this way. The ending leaves something to guess and means: do not be too frivolous about such things.
69789: Around the middle of the 17th century a dead woman appeared, about a year after her death, to her son-in-law, who in his fright, much to his regret, forgot to ask the purpose of her visit. A while later he found his mother-in-law lying in her bed. Now he was calmer and dared to ask what she wanted, whereupon she left the bed and stood before him in a shining white robe. This, and the unmistakable features of her face, frightened him again. She said: There is strife in the family over the division of my estate; I wish you to keep peace among yourselves and divide my goods honestly and unselfishly. The son-in-law promised this. The apparition vanished and did not return, for her wish was fulfilled.
69791: Near the wooded village of Wouterswoude there are footpaths called the Halepaden. Less than forty years ago a naked man haunted them. He had also been seen many years before. He appeared mostly in August, when the crops had been brought in, by day and at dusk as well as at night. Many people in the area had seen him then. He was a man with well-fleshed limbs and smooth black hair, neatly combed. Nobody knew who or what he was, but it was generally believed that he was someone who found no rest after death because of the evil he had done on earth; those who had seen him all declared that he always vanished into a pool or pond near the Halepaden.
69792: Two skippers spend the night on the bank of the Tjonger, which is said to be haunted. The two skippers think they can handle the ghost, but as soon as they have said so, they see the ghost coming towards them. They decide to chase the ghost, but one of them soon becomes frightened. They give up the chase and leave again with their ship.
69793: A girl wants to ferry someone across in her little boat, but it turns out to be a ghost. She is so shaken by this that she dies soon after coming home.
69794: Discussion of second sight. People who know when someone will die, often through a kind of prediction. One example is seeing an event that is yet to take place. People born with a caul have a particular gift for this. They can, for instance, see a funeral procession at night. People born without a caul cannot see this procession, but can still be troubled by it.
69795: If someone walked there at night, he might unexpectedly see a white foal racing past him at full speed, after which it suddenly vanished.
69796: One could also meet an old woman with a little basket on her arm there. The same was true of her: no sooner had she appeared than she was gone again.
69797: In the south of Friesland a funeral procession is called a begangel. Some people can have visions of a benangel. One of these people with second sight once saw the funeral of a farmer in a vision. Against all custom, the hearse was pulled by a white horse. The farmer died and his funeral procession looked exactly as in the seer's vision.
69798: Sape has second sight because he was born with a caul. He sees a man's death and funeral before the man has actually died. Against all custom, a white horse has to be harnessed to the hearse. He tells his vision and everything goes as he saw it.
69799: In 1865, near Poppingawier, a farmer had a vision of a funeral. Over the coffin lay a white sheet, indicating that a woman had died in childbed. To make sure this would not happen to his own wife, he made an alteration to the house. Later he moved away to live elsewhere. His successor undid the alteration, but not long afterwards his wife died in childbed and everything happened exactly as the farmer had seen.
69800: A minister's wife sees her own coffin and funeral. Her husband will not believe her, but when the woman gives birth for the second time, she dies in childbed. Everything goes exactly as she had foreseen, despite the minister's attempts to prevent it.
69801: A skipper once heard a strange sound coming from behind his ship. When he went to investigate, he could find nothing. A long time later, when the skipper sailed past the same spot, he fell from his ship into the water. The sounds he made getting back to the bank were the same as those he had heard before, so he knew it had been a voorspook (a ghostly forewarning).
69802: A farmhand cannot sleep because of a premonition. Every night he sees three men dressing a dead body. One night he decides to find out more and cuts a lock of hair from the dead person so that he can recognise them. The next day it turns out he has cut off his own lock of hair. The farmhand leaves the farm to escape his fate, but years later comes back for a visit. He falls ill and dies. Everything happens exactly as the farmhand had foreseen.
69803: An elderly widow gets the feeling that something terrible will soon happen after hearing strange noises. Not long afterwards the eldest daughter falls fatally ill. When it is thought she will die, the mother walks up the stairs to warn the grandmother. Then the daughter dies. The grandmother declares that the sound of the mother coming up the stairs to tell her the daughter would probably die was the same as the sound she had heard earlier.
69804: People born with a caul sometimes also see at night a house, a mill or another building on fire. If they then have the chance to touch the walls of such a building and find them cold, it will not burn down, but a new building will replace the old one without a fire. If, on the contrary, the walls are warm, it must burn down. This will happen within a short time if the foreshadowing apparition is seen before midnight. If it is seen after midnight, it takes a long time, sometimes years, before the fire comes. This also applies to other night visions. When the begangel (funeral apparition) stands on the graves and no person sees it, the horses that pass the churchyard still see it. They then become skittish, make wild leaps and can easily bolt if the driver is not on his guard.
69805: A seer in Eernewoude saw a steamboat sailing on the broad water beside this village, when no one yet dreamed that steamboats would be put into service from Drachten to Leeuwarden. Likewise, here and there people heard the roar of trains, years before there was any talk of railways in Friesland.
69806: In the north of Ferwerderadeel, a very long time ago, people thought they saw the letters O W N in the sky one evening. Someone with a prophetic spirit read them as: O Woe Netherlands! But a joker was of the opinion that the meaning could also be: O We Nitwits!
69807: Before the sea flood of 1825, a white apparition was sometimes seen at night near Dijken in Doniawerstal, usually resting its elbows on a field gate. After the flood this ghost was no longer seen.
69808: One or more people who are out on the road or still outdoors at night or late in the evening can sometimes hear, at some distance, frightened cries for help that seem to come from a nearby waterway or lake. If they go there, they find there is nothing. But then winter comes; the water freezes and people start skating. Then it is usually the same people who hear the same cries for help again at the same place. But now they really come from people who have fallen through the ice and are in mortal danger. Such accidents announced by voorspook (a ghostly apparition foreshadowing an event) usually end in death.
69809: Some craftsmen hear ghostly sounds when someone is about to die. They hear the knocking and planing of people making a coffin. On one of these occasions she heard a bump against the frame of the front door. This was inexplicable, because the door was quite far from the workshop. But not long afterwards someone died and the event came true, exactly as it had been heard.
69811: A woman in Boyl who believed in predictions claimed one night to have heard the sounds of a parsonage being built there. This took place before there was any talk of Boyl becoming a separate parish. This happened in 1860.
69812: In some farmhouses the churning mill is heard going at night or in the evening. This happens mostly in very old houses, where perhaps for more than a century and a half hundreds of thousands of pounds of butter have been made with the help of the churning mill. Fearless people have sometimes dared to go and investigate. But then they found everything quiet and in its place. Once they had returned to the living room, however, the work started again. It is not advisable to make such an investigation without a light. Whoever dared to do so would stand a good chance of receiving a blow or shove that hit home, without knowing where or from whom this greeting came.
69813: Ghost story about the farm Het Vierhuis, which was said to be uncanny. There was supposedly a room whose door would always open again. One of the farmhands had also heard ghostly noises when he had to spend the night in the stable.
69814: Around 1830 it happened that a poor woman and sorceress named Mone rang at a grand house on the Vliet near Leeuwarden. When no one answered her ringing, she rang again. The door was opened and the woman was snapped at: However long you ring, we give nothing. The beggar woman left, but the house bell kept on jingling, day and night. Everything in the house shook with it. It seems to have stopped again after all, because later nothing more was heard of it.
69819: In the northeast of Schoterland, especially around Jubbega, there are marshy heathlands from which quite a lot of wilde lantaarns (wild lanterns, will-o'-the-wisps) rise. They mostly stay above the spot where they arise, but if one sometimes sees such a little light floating over the road in the dark, there will soon be a death in the village.
69820: The little beetle that can make a ticking sound like a watch in the wood of furniture and panelling indoors is called the "wild watch" in Friesland.
69821: The glow-worm, which is a beautiful glittering green by day and gives off light at night, is called the wilde lantaarn (wild lantern). A swarm of these luminous little creatures can sometimes be seen flying in the dark, and this is actually a wilde lantaarn. Seeing this apparition bodes no more good than the ticking of the wilde horloge (wild clock, a death-watch ticking). Luminous vapours rising from muddy ditches and marsh pools are also called wilde lantaarn.
69822: In the old days an underground yearling calf lived near Molkwerum. Often, when someone in a house was going to die, this calf showed itself outside by the window. This often happened just before the death. It was the devil himself who appeared in this shape.
69823: On Ameland there are still woutermannetjes (little goblins), who prick people in the legs with pins at night. There are also riding tables. Sometimes, by moonlight, little old women are seen walking over the dunes with large cupboards on their backs.
69826: Once a year the werewolf must leave his home to roam about in the shape of a black wolf or tormenting beast. The werewolf is usually furious, especially when he sees something red. Sometimes he can get wounded as a result, or people hit him. He may be left with a mark on his body from this, which can affect his character. He may afterwards be seen as an odd fellow.
69830: There are various ways to ward off a nightmare, including scattering flour. If the nightmare gets flour on her body or clothing, she must stand still until she is discovered in the morning. This is because a nightmare may not and cannot take anything from the house she visits at night. Dry rye grains are also said to work. The nightmare is also said to fear sharp tools. In this way horses can also be protected against the nightmare.
69835: The Zwarteweg, between Leeuwarden and Hardegarijp, has always been very lonely. One can walk there for an hour without seeing houses, except in the distance. In the past, when it was an old sand road, all sorts of things were told about it, and this did not change right away when it became a national highway lined on both sides with dense trees. It is said that someone once met a crying boy there, and when asked why he was crying, the lad answered: "I am afraid that I will become afraid." That is how notorious the Zwarteweg was.
69838: It is said that there are women who have a white liver. A man married to such a woman cannot live long. If a woman happens to marry several times and her husband dies fairly soon, the people around her come to suspect that she has a white liver. Unmarried men would do well not to seek the hand of such a widow.
69839: It is further believed that a person, or an animal, can become murderous if on the road or in the street he happens to step in the footprints of someone who has just committed a murder. This affliction cannot be cured, except by eating a piece of bread cut with the same knife with which the murder was committed.
69840:
In the old days people came up with all sorts of means to counter the devil's work. One of these was placing a grid flat on the ground at the entrance to a churchyard. Cattle, and the devil too because of his horse's hooves, could not cross it without stumbling. A wooden cross that could turn on a spindle was also placed above the grid, so people could pass the spindle one at a time.
The story goes that if something is well arranged, no trouble will come of it. Nowadays there are no grids at churchyards any more, but sometimes there is still a cross.

130218: The devil appears when children look in the mirror.
130223: With the chaplain's help, the bewitchment of the churn, cows and horse is lifted.

130390: Haunting at a spot in a lake.

130404: At night a light can be seen.

130518: The eerie howling of a dog means that someone will die.

130522: A prediction that iron will float on water comes true. Later there are iron ships.

130525: At night a silent ghost comes and suddenly vanishes.

130559: What a man dreams later really happens.

130586: At night noise is heard on a farm.

130623: The devil takes away a skipper after he has received a new ship from Freemasons.
130629: The parsonage is haunted; doors open and close by themselves.

130639: While playing cards, the jack of hearts is pushed out under the window and taken, after which a bottle of liquor is slid inside under the window.

130648: Lights are seen at a spot where houses are later built.
130651: A duivelbanner (exorcist) warns a man who has been given a remedy for a sick child that the remedy must not be seen, and that he may meet a cat on the way. He meets three cats and cannot get rid of them.
130654:
Whoever sees the basilisk emerge bursts apart.
Seeing the future in a black mirror; whoever walks away from the mirror backwards drops dead.
130656: Sighting of a woman dressed in white with a veil, travelling in a spinning butter tub.
130657: Sighting at night of a dog with a death's head.
130658: Someone with a death's head and glowing eyes walking about at night on hands and feet.
130660: In the evening or at night there is banging on the barn door, where nothing can then be seen. The house is later demolished.
130661: During the day two horses stand in the field; in the evening three horses are seen.

130665: The devil, in the shape of a young cow that lives underground, looks through the window when someone lies dying.
130666: Witches change into hares that milk the cows early in the morning.
130667: Duivelbanner (exorcist) frees a child and a butter churn from bewitchment.

130672: A woman born with a caul predicts a death and who will lay the cloth over the coffin, and it comes true.

130675: A lowered and tied-down mast and sails are hoisted at night. After the mast and sails have been lowered and tied down, there is noise again, but everything is in its place. 130678: The naming of a place where an old, bent man returns after his death, looking for the money he buried during his life and could not find again.
130680: Hearing coffin wood being moved at night means someone will die. The way it is moved shows whether heavy or light wood will be used.
130681: A calf tied to a certain staple in the roof beams will die.
130683: The farmhands deny an accusation of neglect in feeding the cattle. When the farmer says that if that is so, the devil may take him, two large black dogs appear. In fear he calls out three times to pray, after which the dogs disappear. Later the farm burns down, and the rebuilt farm burns down too. Both times two black dogs were seen.
130684: A woman dreams of details of the funerals of her husband and son, which then happen in reality.
130686: Meeting a funeral procession in the evening, which stops by a pedestrian who must walk along until the procession stops at a house and disappears. A death then follows in that house.
130687: Haunting on a farm: at midnight buckets rattle but nothing can be seen; a tame horse at the churning mill rears, neighs and is sweaty.
130690: If you walk around the tower three times in the evening and look at the church, on the third time a white figure is seen between the buttresses.
130692: A father forbids a marriage, after which his daughter dies of a broken heart and after her death wanders at the place where she met her beloved. Version in which the father pines away after his daughter's death, finds no rest in his grave and wanders about.
130693: At a haunted spot, a passer-by's hat or cap is demanded.
130695: At a stone bridge a foal is seen with a noose around its neck and a glowing binding stick in its mouth.
130697: On a dark morning near the churchyard, a white figure is seen that stays silent when greeted and suddenly disappears.
130698: Conjuring little soldiers out of the hearth pit, who disappear after marching a round.

130724: A man sees a funeral procession at night in which the men wear black caps. A few days later there is the funeral of someone from a region where men wear black caps at funerals.
130725: A woman clinging to a post after a shipwreck begs beachcombers to help her in exchange for her precious rings. But the beachcombers chop off both her hands to take the rings, and the woman drowns. At night skippers see the woman wandering by the post, so the murder is not forgotten.
130733: A woman is regarded as a witch, because the day after a white cat was shot at, the woman walks around with her head wrapped in a cloth.
130734: A wizard makes a barrel of petroleum that someone is rolling along stop and then roll on again.
130737: Little soldiers come out of the hearth for a man who is sitting reading by the hearth. When he reads the story from back to front, the little soldiers step back into the hearth.
130738: Advice from a devil-banisher (exorcist) as protection against a monster in bed: stuff the stable door shut with rags and then smear it with asafoetida.
130739: Hearing hammering at the neighbours' at midnight, but there is nothing to be seen. Later a chicken coop is built. Hearing the scraping of skates when there is no ice; a few days later there is skating. Hearing the sound of trains that do not come.
130744: A wizard fixes a horse and wagon to the spot, walks to the wagon, whereupon the horse starts to run.
130746: When a boy reads a book at a woman's house, cats come out of the hearth, and they go back when the woman reads the book from back to front.
130747: After something has flown across the road, a boy falls and lies stiff. He has to stay in bed and makes strange noises, but calms down when there are glowing gnats in the evening.
130749: A man born with a caul gets up at night to see a funeral; not long afterwards someone is buried.
130752: People never walk in the middle of the road because of funeral processions, because of the danger of, for example, having to walk over the hearse or being picked up and thrown into a ditch.
130753: A prediction that a train would run in the canal did not come true.
130755: A shroud must be somewhat shorter to leave the feet bare, otherwise they get dirty and the dead cannot find rest.
130758: A nightmare in the form of a black cat that comes from the feet up to the throat. After the cat is seized and told who is boss, it disappears.
130759: A child stiffens and cries in the evenings. After devil's dung is put in its clothes, the stiffening and crying stop. An old woman remarks that the child was crying. A move to a house where a child died after, according to its mother, being bewitched by an old woman.

130761: The dead get no rest if the shroud was sewn on a Sunday.
130762: A woman who it is hoped will stay away after the birth of a child comes anyway. The child refuses to drink, although the mother has enough milk and the neighbour's child does drink from her. The woman comes often; notably she never opens the box-bed door at the head end. After some time her daughter comes, and then the child will drink from its mother.
130764: A woman strikes a cat that crosses its front paws, whereupon the cat flies at the woman. Later it turns out that a witch is lying wounded in bed.
130766: Some people can make ducks or geese come out of the hearth pit.
130767: The narrator's grandfather and sister can hear from the ringing of the church bells whether there will be a funeral within three days.
130769: The part of the shroud around the neck is made last. The needle must not be removed from it, otherwise the dead cannot find rest.
130772: Placing a daalder (silver coin) at the bottom of the churn to lift the bewitchment of the churn.
130774: People who sell their soul to the devil go to a crossroads where they sell a black cat for a daalder (coin). Someone has a boot with money, but out of regret removes the sole, so that the boot can never become full.
130777: People believe they hear witches sewing at night, but don't dare to look.
130778: A black dog that walks along with a peddler must have been the devil.
130781: A man often sees a funeral procession at night; a few days later there is a funeral.
130782: During a polecat hunt the dogs are afraid; one dog even runs home.
130783: On a spot where men hear hammering at night and see a timber frame standing, though there is nothing there, a farm is later built.
130784: Dogs will not go after a polecat; an old woman who is spoken to says there is nothing there, but she must have been the polecat.
130796: Making little soldiers come out of the stove.
130799: A woman hears wailing without anything to be seen. A few days later a girl and her mother drown.
130800: In the evening a farmer's wife hears a crowd of people on the canal, but there is nothing to be seen. Later there is ice with a mass of people on it, and someone drowns. The dead person is brought to the farm.
130801: A docile horse turns around and will not go on. The cause is said to be a passing funeral procession. A week later someone dies whose funeral goes along the same route.
130802: Correct prediction of a child's sex.
130803: A woman knows of a death in advance.
130804: One magpie by the house means misfortune, two magpies mean there is news.
130806: Young women don't dare pass a culvert in the evening for fear of bewitchment.
130807: Fear of a foal with a porridge pot around its neck and of a black dog.
130811: A man thinks he hears a witch and children at night.
130812: Little soldiers come out of the hearth pit when someone reads from a book of magic. To get them back into the hearth pit, the owner must get rid of the book.
130813: A woman's dream comes true: a hearse with a large coffin, and men she knows carrying the coffin into the house.
130815: Handcuffs fall from a wizard's wrists and the lock falls out of the door when the wizard is locked up.
130818: A maidservant who watches what happens at night to a horse that stands with braided mane in the morning notices that at midnight the horse makes a noise, and when she makes a light she sees a woman on the horse.
130820: At night a woman sees a coffin standing crosswise on the road.
130830: Asafoetida (devil's dung) in the turn-up of a trouser leg as protection against witchcraft and ghost dogs.
130831: Stepping aside for a funeral procession at night, and someone will surely die.
130835: A man who told a duivelbanner (exorcist) that he will beat a witch to death hears more and more noise as he approaches his house. Inside it is quiet, but the witches beat on the windows.
130836: Cats around the house disappear when the father of crying children threatens to stab them to death.
130837: Cats that prowl around the house cannot be hit. A man believes his sick sheep is bewitched and wants to have it slaughtered. The butcher throws something into the sheep's pen and after a while says the sheep should be given something to eat. Then the sheep gets up, healthy.
130844: Suspicion that a corpse has not stiffened.
130846: Noise is heard, but when people go to look, nothing is wrong.
130847: Although there are only sand roads, horses are heard trotting on a paved road in the evening.
130852: The fire of a house was seen years beforehand.
130853: A black dog accompanies a woman to her house, snaps at her and vanishes.
130854: Scattering flour on the bed board to ward off the nightmare and other ghosts.
130857: Walking at the side of the road at night so as not to be pushed aside by a funeral procession.
130859: Music and singing are heard from the sky at night.
130860: Talk about white women (ghosts), wild lanterns (will-o'-the-wisps) and wreaths in the pillows of the sick.
130862: A blasphemer is picked up and flung across the ditch.
130863: A dead person who cannot find rest haunts at night.
130865: Doors are heard slamming in a house in the evening.
130866: A man born with a caul warns people to step aside for a funeral procession he sees. Seeing a funeral procession is also an omen of a funeral shortly afterwards.
130867: Ghosts take away clothing that was laid under a tree.
130868: At a place where little lights are seen as if ships were sailing, a canal was later dug.
130876: Witch keeps a wooden doll full of pins and puts the doll in the hearth pit.
130878: Seeing the Northern Lights means war is coming.
130882: A black dog howls for three evenings at the house of a sick person; after the death the dog has vanished.
130883: A few days before someone dies, a man born with a caul sees a funeral procession on a wall.
130886: A nightmare (night spirit) sails across a lake in a butter churn and attacks someone; it comes in through the keyhole.
130890: Where will-o'-the-wisps go out, an accident will happen.
130891: A mushroom is found in a goat's brain.
130892: Wreaths found in a pillow must be burnt.
130898: Building a farmhouse in one night is the devil's work. When the cock crows, the farmhouse is finished except for the owl board. After fitting a wooden owl board fails several times, a stone owl board is put in place.
130902: A farmer hits a cat with a club; the cat is often near the sty of a pig that will not grow. Afterwards a witch has a wounded arm.
130904: Black dog that disappears from a woman when she gets home, after which she feels ill.
130907: After the body of a poisoned woman is examined, a rumour arises that the head and entrails were removed. Shortly afterwards, at night, there is an encounter with a woman in white without a head.
130908: A minister sends someone to a wonder doctor for his wife. The wonder doctor gives him a remedy and says that the wife will be set over the hedge three times when she takes the remedy.
